He called to First Woman, Water Sprinkler, and Black God, and together they shaped the six sacred mountains from the Third World soil, each one placed in a cardinal or intermediate direction, each one adorned with the materials and spirits of its realm.

In the East, they raised Sisnaajiní — Blanca Peak. They decorated it with white shells, white lightning, and white corn. Dark clouds gathered around its summit for male rain. Rock Crystal Boy and Crystal Girl became its resident spirits, their bodies gleaming like the mountain itself.

In the South, they placed Tsoodził — Mount Taylor. They adorned it with turquoise, dark mist, and animals of every kind. Light clouds drifted around it for female rain. Turquoise Boy and Corn Girl made their home there.

In the West, Dookʼoʼoosłííd — the San Francisco Peaks — received abalone shell and yellow corn. The sun set behind it each evening, painting the sky in colors that mirrored the mountain's adornment.

In the North, Dibé Nitsaa — Hesperus Mountain — was covered with black beads and heavy rain. The winter winds blew from its peak, and the darkness of the longest night seemed to emanate from its slopes.

At each mountain, they created resident deities — beings who would tend the sacred sites and channel the powers of the directions to the people. They placed stones and crystals at each peak, each one a repository of spiritual energy.

Then First Man stood at the center and drew a circle in the dirt. "This is the middle," he said. "The mountains surround it. The people will live here, at the center, protected by the powers of all six directions."

The Holy People blessed the mountains and the land between them. And when the ceremony was complete, the Fourth World had a shape — not flat and featureless anymore, but ringed with sacred peaks that held the world together like the posts of a great lodge.

title: The Hero Twins: Monster Slayer and Child of the Water
summary: In Navajo mythology, Changing Woman gave birth to the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) and Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní), fathered by the Sun. The twins were born to rid the world of monsters (anaye) that terrorized the people. They journeyed to their father the Sun, passing tests of strength and courage. The Sun tried to kill them with a sweat lodge of stone knives, a heated stone bed, and poisoned smoke, but Spider Woman protected them. They received lightning arrows and armor before returning to earth. Monster Slayer killed the giant Yéʼiitsoh by striking his leg armor and then his head with arrows. He and his brother slew Déélgééd the Horned Monster by shooting arrows into his body and causing him to fall into the ocean. They disposed of other monsters including the giant birds, the monster who kicked people off cliffs, and those who caused hunger, poverty, cold, and old age. Some monsters were allowed to remain in diminished form as a balance for humanity.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897); Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956)
full_text:
Changing Woman gave birth to two sons — Monster Slayer, Naayéé' Neizghání, and Child of the Water, Tóbájíshchíní — fathered by the Sun himself. They were born to rid the world of the anaye, the monsters that had been born during the separation of men and women and that had been devouring the people ever since.

The twins grew with terrifying speed. Within weeks they were hunting with bows made of lightning. But they needed weapons powerful enough to kill beings that ordinary arrows could not wound. They decided to journey to the sky to visit their father, the Sun.

The journey was long and filled with tests. The Sun tried to kill them — not out of cruelty, but to prove their worthiness. He built a sweat lodge of stone knives and heated it until the air inside was white with steam. The twins entered and survived. He laid them on a bed of heated stones that should have burned them to ash. They slept through the night and woke unharmed. He filled the lodge with poisoned smoke that would have killed any mortal. Spider Woman breathed a counter-charm through the smoke holes, and the twins survived that too.

Satisfied, the Sun gave them lightning arrows — shafts of pure energy tipped with flint points that could cut through anything — and armor that gleamed like water. "Go back to the earth," he said, "and destroy the anaye."

Monster Slayer found Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, wearing armor of flint knives on his legs. The Sun had weakened the giant with four strikes, and Monster Slayer finished him — first arrow to break the leg armor, second to shatter it, third through the head, fourth to pin his hair to the ground when he tried to rise.

He and his brother slew Déélgééd the Horned Monster by shooting arrows into its body until it fell into the ocean. They destroyed the giant birds, the cliff-kicker, the monsters of hunger and poverty and cold.

But they did not kill everything. When Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger begged for their lives, the twins listened to their arguments and allowed them to remain in diminished form. The world needed balance. Without suffering, there would be no appreciation for joy.

The monsters were gone. The people were safe. And the twins returned to the sky, where they still stand as guardians against the darkness.

title: The Slaying of Yéʼiitsoh
summary: Monster Slayer's greatest feat in Navajo tradition was killing Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, who wore armor of flint knives on his legs. The Hero Twins approached him after their father the Sun had weakened the giant by striking him four times. Monster Slayer shot an arrow into the giant's leg armor but it shattered; a second arrow broke through. The giant collapsed face-down, and Monster Slayer shot a third arrow through his head. Child of the Water also shot the giant's head. When Yéʼiitsoh began to rise again, Spider Woman warned the twins. Monster Slayer shot a fourth arrow which pinned the giant's hair to the ground. As Yéʼiitsoh died, rivers of blood flowed from his wounds. Monster Slayer used the giant's own stone knife to cut off his head and returned home carrying it as a trophy.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
Of all the monsters the Hero Twins destroyed, none was more feared than Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant. He stood taller than a cottonwood tree, his skin the color of dried blood, and across his legs he wore armor made of flint knives — each blade sharper than a hawk's talon, each one capable of slicing through stone.

The people had tried to fight him. Warriors charged with spears and arrows, and the flint armor shattered their weapons like dry twigs. Yéʼiitsoh laughed as he devoured them, his jaws opening wide enough to swallow a man whole.

The Sun had been watching. From his path across the sky, he struck Yéʼiitsoh four times with bolts of lightning, weakening the giant's armor and slowing his movements. Then the Hero Twins came.

Monster Slayer approached first. He carried a bow of lightning and arrows tipped with flint that could cut through anything — or so he believed. He drew and fired at the giant's leg. The arrow struck the flint armor and shattered into dust.

A second arrow. This one was different — blessed by Spider Woman, its tip made of the same flint as the giant's armor but consecrated with songs of destruction. It struck the leg armor and broke through, sending shards of flint flying. The giant staggered, his leg buckling.

Yéʼiitsoh fell forward, face-down in the dust. Monster Slayer shot a third arrow through the back of his head. Child of the Water shot a fourth through his skull from the other side. The arrows met inside the giant's brain.

But Yéʼiitsoh was not dead yet. Spider Woman's voice came from everywhere and nowhere: "He will rise again if you do not pin him down." Monster Slayer shot a fifth arrow that pinned the giant's hair to the earth. The great body shuddered once and was still.

Rivers of blood flowed from the giant's wounds, carving channels in the earth that would become the arroyos of the Navajo homeland. Monster Slayer took the giant's own stone knife — the one he had used to sharpen his flint armor — and cut off his head.

He carried the head back to the people. It was so large it took four men to lift it. They placed it on a rock outside the village, and for a long time it served as a warning: this is what happens to those who prey upon the people.

title: The Slaying of Déélgééd the Horned Monster
summary: After defeating Yéʼiitsoh, the Hero Twins faced Déélgééd, the Horned Monster, a creatures described as having one horn and living in the water. In some versions the monster was a giant water creature with a single horn. Monster Slayer and Child of the Water tracked it to its lair. Monster Slayer shot the creature multiple times; its blood gushed out and it plunged into the ocean. As it floated on the surface, both twins shot arrows into it until it was dead. The head of Déélgééd floated to the shore where people later used its horn for ceremonies. This victory was one of several that cleared the world of the monsters that had been devouring the people since the time of the separation of men and women.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
The Horned Monster — Déélgééd — lived in the deep water, in the lightless places where the river met the underground springs. It had a single horn rising from its skull like a tower of bone, and its body was long and serpentine, covered in scales that reflected no light.

People who came near the water disappeared. Fishermen found only their empty canoes, spun in circles by the creature's wake. Children who played at the river's edge were pulled under by currents that had no natural source. The monster's horn broke the surface sometimes — a pale spike cutting through the water like a sail — and those who saw it ran.

Monster Slayer and Child of the Water tracked the creature for seven days, following the trail of missing people and the signs that only the Holy People could read — disturbed water, dead fish floating belly-up, the sour smell of the creature's breath rising from the river in bubbles.

They found its lair in a deep pool beneath a cliff. Monster Slayer shot an arrow into the water. It struck something solid, and the pool erupted. Déélgééd rose from the depths, its horn gleaming, its mouth open wide enough to swallow a horse.

Monster Slayer shot again. The arrow pierced the creature's side, and blood — dark, thick, almost black — gushed into the water. The monster dove, trying to escape, but Child of the Water was waiting underwater. He shot an arrow through the creature's belly from below.

Déélgééd surfaced one last time, thrashing so violently that the waves crested over the banks. Both twins shot arrows into its body — three, four, five — until the creature was pinned to the surface by the sheer number of shafts protruding from its flesh.

The monster died slowly, its great body floating on the water like a fallen tree. Its horn washed ashore weeks later, and the Holy People used it in ceremonies for generations — a reminder that the waters held power, and that power could be dangerous.

The pool where Déélgééd died is said to be deeper than any other body of water in the Fourth World. The people do not fish there. They do not let their children play near its banks. They leave offerings at the water's edge — turquoise and cornmeal — and speak softly when they pass.

title: The Story of Noqoilpi the Great Gambler
summary: In Navajo tradition, Noqoilpi was a powerful gambler who challenged and defeated all who came to him, taking their possessions and even their freedom. He was said to live at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí (Great Spruce Mountain or El Capitan). Noqoilpi gambled with entire nations, winning their wealth and enslaving their people. The Holy People decided he had grown too powerful and needed to be stopped. They sent a challenger who gambled with Noqoilpi in a series of contests. The challenger, aided by the Holy People, finally beat Noqoilpi at the moccasin game and other gambling games. Defeated, Noqoilpi was forced to leave the Navajo world. He departed eastward, taking his gambling implements with him, and was never seen again, though his influence lingered in the form of gambling as a human vice.
source: Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956)
full_text:
Noqoilpi lived at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí — Great Spruce Mountain — in a house of polished stone where the gambling games never stopped. He was beautiful, charming, and utterly without mercy. His smile could convince anyone to play, and his luck was supernatural — the stones always fell where he wanted them, the sticks always landed in his favor.

People came from every direction to challenge him. Warriors came, certain their skill would triumph. Chiefs came, bringing the wealth of their nations. Young men came, proud and certain. One by one, they played. One by one, they lost.

Noqoilpi took everything. Their horses, their weapons, their clothes. Then he took their freedom. The losers became his servants, building his house, cooking his food, carrying his gambling implements. He enslaved entire nations with nothing but a game of chance and a smile.

The Holy People watched. They saw the people enslaved, saw the wealth of many nations piling up at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí. They decided Noqoilpi had gone too far.

They sent a challenger — a man of no particular appearance, carrying no particular wealth. He walked into Noqoilpi's house and sat down across from the great gambler.

They played the moccasin game. Noqoilpi won the first round. The challenger smiled and played again. He won the second. And the third. And the fourth. Each time, the stakes grew higher. Noqoilpi's confidence wavered. His smile faltered.

In the final round, the challenger won everything — Noqoilpi's wealth, his servants, his house, even the clothes off his back.

Noqoilpi stood naked and defeated. The Holy People commanded him to leave the Navajo world forever. He gathered his gambling sticks and his stones and walked eastward, disappearing over the horizon. He was never seen again.

But his influence lingered. The games he left behind — the moccasin game, the stick game, the guessing games — became part of Navajo life. And the people tell this story to remind themselves: gambling is the vice of Noqoilpi, and those who play too long may lose more than they can afford.

title: The Story of the Moccasin Game
summary: The Moccasin Game is a traditional Navajo story explaining the origin of a sacred winter game. In the mythological account, the animals gathered to play the moccasin game, which involves hiding a stone or yucca ball under one of four moccasins while the opposing side guesses its location. The game was played between the day animals and the night animals, with the stakes being control over light and darkness. Through trickery and strategy — particularly from Coyote who cheated by using a yucca ring instead of a stone — the night animals won, establishing that darkness would have its place in the world. This story is traditionally told only during winter months and is considered sacred, teaching lessons about balance, trickery, and the boundaries between day and night, summer and winter.
source: Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956); Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
The animals gathered in a clearing on a cold winter night to play the moccasin game — Yéʼiiʼ — the sacred game that determines the balance between light and dark, summer and winter. The day animals took one side, the night animals the other.

The rules were simple: four moccasins lay in a row on the ground. A small stone — or a ball of yucca fiber — was hidden under one of them. The opposing side had to guess which moccasin held the stone. If they guessed right, they won a point. If they guessed wrong, the hiding side won.

The night animals were winning. The day animals grew desperate. Coyote, who sat among the night animals, saw their distress. He was supposed to help his side, but Coyote's loyalty was always to himself first.

He took a ring of yucca fiber and slipped it under his own moccasin instead of the stone. When the day animals guessed his moccasin, they found only the ring — no stone. They lost the point. Coyote grinned.

But the game went on. The night animals' lead grew. The day animals played harder, drawing on every scrap of cunning they possessed. The moccasins were shuffled, the stone was moved, the guesses came faster.

In the end, the night animals won. Darkness had its place. Winter had its season. The world was not meant to be all light or all dark — it needed both, cycling through the year like breath through a body.

The story is told only during winter months, when the nights are long and the stories are old. It is sacred because it explains the deepest mystery of the world: why summer gives way to winter, why day surrenders to night, and why the cycle never ends.

Children listen with wide eyes. Elders speak the words in the old way, their voices rising and falling with the rhythm of the game. And when the story is finished, everyone knows their place in the world a little better.

title: The Maiden Who Became a Bear
summary: A Navajo story about a young woman who transformed into a bear after being mistreated by her family or community. The maiden wandered into the wilderness in despair, and as she walked, her hands and feet slowly transformed into bear claws, her body grew fur, and she became a powerful bear. She later encountered hunters from her village, who recognized her by the remnants of her human appearance. The story serves as a cautionary tale about the treatment of others and carries ceremonial significance related to the Mountain Top Chant ceremony. Bear holds special power in Navajo tradition, and this story explains the deep spiritual connection between bears and specific healing ceremonies.
source: Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956); Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
She was young and her name has been forgotten, which is part of the story. She lived in a village where the elders were kind and the children were cruel, as children sometimes are. They mocked her for her quiet ways, for her habit of walking alone at the edge of the village where the forest began.

One evening, after a particularly harsh day of taunting, she walked into the wilderness. She did not take food or water. She did not look back. The trees closed behind her like a curtain.

She walked for three days. On the first day, her hands began to change — her fingers thickening, her nails curving into dark claws. On the second day, fur crept up her arms and across her shoulders, warm and coarse. On the third day, she dropped to all fours and ran.

She was a bear now. Not a woman who had become a bear, but a bear who had once been a woman. The memories were still there, dim and distant, like firelight seen through deep water.

Years later, a hunting party from her old village tracked a great bear to its den. When the lead hunter looked into the bear's eyes, he saw something human there — a recognition, a sadness. "It is her," he whispered. "The one who walked away."

The bear looked at the hunters and did not flee. She turned and walked deeper into the forest, and the hunters let her go.

The story became part of the Mountain Top Chant — the ceremony that heals those who have been touched by animal spirits. When a person falls ill after an encounter with a bear, the medicine man sings the songs the bear woman learned in the wilderness, and the boundary between human and animal is made clear again.

Bear holds great power in Navajo tradition. The bear is not merely an animal but a being who exists on the threshold between the human world and the spirit world. To harm a bear without proper ceremony is to invite transformation — the kind that cannot be reversed.

title: The Mountain Top Chant
summary: The Mountain Top Chant (Dzil Naʼoodilii) is a major Navajo ceremony whose origin story tells of a maiden who encountered a bear during her puberty ceremony. A young Navajo woman, while gathering materials for her ceremony, was approached by a bear who taught her the sacred songs, prayers, and sandpaintings of the Mountain Top Chant. The bear spirit took her into the mountains where she learned the entire ceremonial cycle over several days. When she returned to her people, she taught them the ceremony, which is used to invoke the protection and power of the mountain spirits and to cure illnesses caused by animals. The nine-day ceremony features elaborate sandpaintings, songs, and dances that reenact the maiden's journey and transformation.
source: Washington Matthews, The Mountain Chant: A Navajo Ceremony (1887)
full_text:
The Mountain Top Chant — Dzil Naʼoodilii — began with a girl and a bear, as many sacred things begin with something unexpected.

A young Navajo woman was preparing for her puberty ceremony when she wandered into the high country to gather the materials she would need — pine boughs, sacred corn pollen, the white shell that represented her connection to the East. The mountain air was thin and cold, and the pines stood like sentinels along the ridge.

The bear found her there. It was not the kind of bear that runs from humans. It stood on its hind legs and spoke in a voice like wind through hollow reeds. "I have come to teach you," the bear said. "You will learn songs that heal. You will learn sandpaintings that restore the broken places in people's bodies and spirits."

For seven days, the bear taught her. Each morning, they climbed higher into the mountains. Each night, the bear sang songs that made the stones vibrate and the stars lean closer. The girl learned the nine days of the ceremony — the songs, the prayers, the sandpaintings that map the Holy People's journey through the sacred mountains.

She learned that the sandpaintings are not art but medicine — each line a prayer, each color a direction, each figure a Holy Person who can be called upon to restore balance. The paintings are made on the floor of the healing lodge, and when the ceremony is complete, they are swept away, their power absorbed into the patient.

When she returned to her people, she taught them the ceremony. And so the Mountain Top Chant entered the Navajo healing tradition, used to cure illnesses caused by bears and other animals — the sickness that comes from disturbing a bear's den, from stepping on a bear's track, from encountering a bear in the wrong way at the wrong time.

The ceremony lasts nine days. The medicine man sings hundreds of songs. Sandpaintings appear and disappear like dreams. And when it is over, the patient rises, healed, and walks back into the world carrying a gratitude that extends to the bear who first taught the songs in the high country where the pines stand like sentinels and the air tastes of snow.

title: The White Bead Maiden's Marriage to the Sun
summary: In this Navajo story, White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́) was sought in marriage by the Sun. The Sun, disguised as a handsome warrior, courted the maiden. After many trials, she agreed to marry him and traveled to his house in the eastern horizon. The Sun's house was a square room of turquoise and white shell with the four directions represented. White Bead Maiden bore the Sun's children, who became the Hero Twins. However, the Sun already had another wife, and tensions arose in their celestial household. White Bead Maiden eventually returned to earth, where she was transformed into Changing Woman, the central female deity of Navajo religion who governs the cycles of life, seasons, and time itself. This story establishes the sacred lineage from the Sun to the Navajo people and the deep connection between celestial and earthly realms.
source: Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956)
full_text:
White Bead Maiden — Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ — lived in the Third World before the flood, in a village near the Crossing of the Waters. She was beautiful in the way that white shell is beautiful — pale, luminous, with a light that seemed to come from within rather than from the sun above.

The Sun saw her. From his path across the sky, he watched her walking along the river, her white shell body catching his rays and throwing them back like mirrors. He loved her from that distance, the way one loves a song heard through water — faintly, achingly.

He came to her in human form, a young man wrapped in light so bright she had to shield her eyes. He courted her with gifts of turquoise and eagle feathers. He told her stories of the sky world, where the houses were made of light and the rivers ran with liquid star. After many days, she agreed to marry him.

She traveled to his house in the eastern horizon, where the sun rises each morning. The house was square and beautiful, built of turquoise and white shell, with the four directions marked on its walls. There she bore him twin sons — Monster Slayer and Child of the Water — who would grow up to destroy the monsters of the Fourth World.

But the Sun already had another wife. Jealousy grew in the celestial household like a disease. The other wife whispered against White Bead Maiden, and the Sun, torn between his loves, grew cold.

White Bead Maiden returned to earth. She walked out of the eastern horizon and down the mountain, carrying nothing but her two sons. When she reached the ground, she was no longer White Bead Maiden. She had become Changing Woman — Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé — the woman who changes with the seasons, who ages and renews, who represents the eternal cycle of life.

She settled on the western ocean, where she built a floating house of turquoise and abalone. And from there, she watches over the Navajo people, aging through the winter and reborn each spring, a reminder that even the Sun's love cannot contain the power of a woman who chooses to change.

title: Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger
summary: After the Hero Twins killed the major monsters, four lesser monsters remained: Old Age (Są́), Cold (Dǫǫh), Poverty (Téʼéʼį́), and Hunger (Báhí). When the twins confronted these beings, they pleaded for their lives. Old Age argued that without him, the world would become overcrowded and people would not appreciate youth. Cold said he was necessary to remind people of their mortality. Poverty claimed his existence motivated people to work and share. Hunger argued that without him, people would not appreciate food. The Hero Twins, acknowledging the necessity of balance in the world, allowed these four to remain in reduced form as part of the natural order of human existence, explaining why humans continue to experience aging, cold, poverty, and hunger.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
After the Hero Twins destroyed the great monsters — Yéʼiitsoh, Déélgééd, the giant birds, the cliff-kicker — four lesser monsters remained. They were not large or fearsome. They did not devour people or destroy villages. They were simply there, crouching at the edges of the world like shadows that would not lift.

Old Age — Są́ — sat in the corner of every dwelling, his breath thin and cold. Cold — Dǫǫh — clung to the bones of the elderly and the exposed. Poverty — Téʼéʼį́ — whispered that there was never enough. Hunger — Báhí — gnawed at the belly even after a full meal.

Monster Slayer found them and raised his lightning arrows. But they did not run. They stood before him, small and trembling, and they spoke.

Old Age said: "If you destroy me, the world will fill with people until there is no room to walk. The old will remain in their prime forever, and the young will never be born. Without me, there is no wisdom, for wisdom comes from the years that aging brings."

Cold said: "If you destroy me, people will forget their mortality. They will take no shelter, make no preparation, waste the gifts of summer. I remind them that comfort is temporary and must be cherished."

Poverty said: "If you destroy me, people will hoard and never share. They will not know the joy of giving, for giving comes from having less than you need. I make the community care for its own."

Hunger said: "If you destroy me, people will eat without gratitude. They will waste food and forget that every meal is a gift. I make them pray before they eat. I make them thank the buffalo and the corn and the rain."

Monster Slayer listened. His brother listened. The arguments were sound. The world required balance — not perpetual joy, but the full range of human experience.

They lowered their weapons. "You may remain," Monster Slayer said, "but only in diminished form. You will trouble the people, but you will not destroy them. You will remind them, but you will not break them."

And so Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger became part of the natural order — permanent companions to every human life, unwelcome but necessary, like the winter that makes the spring worth celebrating.

title: Departure of Changing Woman
summary: In Navajo tradition, after the monsters were defeated and the world was made safe, Changing Woman decided to leave the earth. She gathered the Holy People and announced her departure to the West. She created a beautiful floating house made of turquoise, abalone shell, white shell, and jet, located on an island in the western ocean. Before leaving, she blessed the Navajo people and gave them the corn, sheep, and knowledge they would need to prosper. She taught them the ceremonies that would protect and heal them. Changing Woman decreed that she would live in the west forever, aging through the winter and rejuvenating each spring — thus establishing the cycle of seasons. She promised to watch over the Navajo people from her western home and to send her blessings whenever the proper ceremonies were performed.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897)
full_text:
The day came when Changing Woman knew it was time to leave. She was old again — winter old, with white hair and skin like crumpled paper — and she called the Holy People to the shore.

"I am going west," she said. "To a place where the ocean meets the sky, where the sun sleeps at night. I have built a house there — turquoise on the outside, abalone on the inside, white shell for the floor and jet for the door. It floats on the water like a prayer boat, and it will be my home forever."

The people wept. Children clung to her robes. Even the Holy People bowed their heads.

"Do not weep," she told them. "I am not dying. I am going to live forever in a different way. Each year, I will age through the winter, just as I have done here. Each spring, I will be young again. The seasons you see — the fall of leaves, the snow, the first green shoot — these are my breath, my heartbeat, the turning of my body."

She blessed the corn fields, laying her hands on the stalks and whispering prayers that made the ears swell with milk. She blessed the sheep, touching each one on the head. She taught the people the ceremonies they would need — the Blessing Way, the songs of protection and renewal — and gave them the knowledge of how to perform them correctly.

"When you are in trouble," she said, "perform the ceremonies I have taught you. I will hear you from the west, and I will send my blessings on the wind."

She walked into a boat made of light and drifted toward the horizon. The people watched from the shore until she was a speck, then a point of light, then nothing. But the sun set in the place where she had gone, and the colors of the western sky — red and gold and deep purple — are Changing Woman's house, glowing with the light of her fire.

Every autumn, when the leaves turn gold and the wind grows cold, the Navajo know that Changing Woman is aging. Every spring, when the first warm breeze blows from the west and the lambs are born, they know she has been reborn.

She is still there, in her house of turquoise and abalone, watching over the people she loved enough to leave.

title: Tawa Creates the Worlds
summary: In the Hopi creation story, in the beginning only Tawa, the Sun Spirit, existed in endless space (Tokpella). Tawa formed the First World but its insect-like creatures lived unhappily in caves. To improve things, Tawa created Sotuknang, his nephew, who in turn created Spider Woman (Spider Grandmother) as a messenger and helper. Spider Woman was sent to lead the first creatures — then resembling insects — to the Second World, where they took on animal forms of wolves and bears. Still dissatisfied, Tawa created a Third World and Spider Woman guided the creatures there, where they finally became human. Spider Woman taught them weaving and pottery, and Hummingbird brought them the fire drill. This cycle of creation, destruction, and renewal through four worlds is central to Hopi cosmology, with humanity now living in the Fourth World.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Barry Pritzker, The Hopi (2011); Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis
full_text:
In the beginning, before the world had shape or name, only Tawa existed — the Sun Spirit, a being of pure light suspended in Tokpella, the Endless Space. There was no earth, no sky, no water. Only Tawa, burning quietly in the void like a coal that refuses to die.

Tawa formed the First World from his own light, shaping it the way a dreamer shapes a dream. The creatures that lived there were small and insect-like, burrowing in caves beneath a sky that had no sun. They were unhappy in their darkness, whispering to each other about the light they had never seen.

To help them, Tawa created his nephew Sotuknang — a being of structure and purpose. Sotuknang in turn created Spider Woman, Spider Grandmother, as a messenger and helper. She was ancient and wise, with legs like the rays of the dawn and eyes that could see in every direction at once.

Spider Woman gathered the First World creatures and led them to the Second World, where they took on the forms of wolves and bears. Still the world was not right — too wild, too cold, too full of teeth.

They climbed to the Third World, where the creatures finally became human. Spider Woman taught them to weave cloth and shape pottery. Hummingbird — a tiny, reckless being with iridescent wings — stole the fire drill from the fire spirits and brought it to the people. For the first time, they had warmth and cooked food.

But the people grew wicked. They fought. They forgot the prayers. And so the Third World was destroyed — in some versions by flood, in others by fire — and the survivors climbed through a hollow reed into the Fourth World, the world we know.

There they met Masauwu, the Spirit of Death and Earth God, who wore a mask that was both hideous and beautiful. He gave them the land and four sacred tablets — instructions for how to live, where to settle, and what ceremonies to perform. And the Fourth World began.

title: The Sipapu Emergence
summary: In one version of the Hopi emergence story, the people of the Third World grew wicked and corrupt. With the help of Spider Grandmother or bird spirits, a hollow bamboo reed grew at the opening between the Third World and the Fourth World. This opening, called the sipapu, is traditionally located at the Grand Canyon. Only the people with good hearts — those who showed kindness — were able to make the journey through the sipapu to the Fourth World, the world of the present. In the Fourth World, they encountered Masauwu, the Spirit of Death and Earth God, who wore a hideous but also beautiful mask. Masauwu gave them their land and four sacred tablets outlining their way of life and their future wanderings. He taught them to worship properly and ensured the dead would return safely to the underworld.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis
full_text:
The people of the Third World had grown wicked. They stole from each other. They forgot the songs that held the world together. They mocked the spirits and ignored the sacred fires. The sky darkened with their bad deeds, and the ground shook beneath their feet.

Spider Grandmother saw what was happening and wept. She went to Tawa and pleaded: "Save the ones who still have good hearts. Let the wicked face the flood, but spare the kind."

Tawa agreed. At the center of the Third World, where a great spring bubbled up from the earth, Spider Grandmother commanded a hollow bamboo reed to grow. It pushed upward through the ground, through the rock, through the darkness between worlds, until its tip emerged into the Fourth World like a green finger pointing at the sky.

The people gathered around the reed. Spider Grandmother looked at them with old eyes. "Only those who have shown kindness," she said. "Only those who have shared their food, who have helped their neighbors, who have spoken truthfully. The reed will not open for the wicked."

One by one, the good people climbed inside. The reed was narrow, and the climb was long — through three worlds of darkness, past rivers of fire and walls of stone. Some people could not make the journey. The reed rejected them, its walls closing tight around those whose hearts were heavy with cruelty.

At the top, they emerged into the Fourth World through an opening called the sipapu — traditionally located at the Grand Canyon, though different villages claim different locations. They found themselves on a small island in a vast ocean, blinking in light they had never seen.

Masauwu was waiting for them. He wore his terrible mask and carried four tablets. "This is your land," he said. "These are your instructions. Follow them, and you will prosper. Forget them, and you will wander."

The people took the tablets and walked into the Fourth World. Behind them, the sipapu closed. The Third World was gone. But the people carried its memory in their ceremonies, in the songs they sang at dawn, in the prayers they whispered before planting corn.

title: The Great Flood and the Voyage to the Fourth World
summary: In the alternative Hopi emergence story, mainly told at Oraibi, Tawa destroyed the Third World in a great flood because of the people's wickedness. Before the destruction, Spider Grandmother sealed the more righteous people inside hollow reeds, which floated as boats. After the waters receded, the survivors found themselves on a small piece of dry land with nothing but water in every direction. They planted a giant bamboo shoot and climbed it to survey the land, but still saw only water. Spider Woman then instructed them to make boats from more reeds. Using island stepping-stones, the people sailed east until they reached the mountainous coasts of the Fourth World. The Hopi Water Clan's name (Patkinyamu) means 'dwelling-on-water,' preserving the memory of this ocean voyage. Different stories (sipapu vs. flood journey) coexist among different Hopi villages.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis
full_text:
In the villages around Oraibi — one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in North America — the elders tell a different story of how the people came to the Fourth World. This is the flood story.

Tawa saw the wickedness of the Third World and decided to destroy it. But before the destruction, Spider Grandmother chose the righteous and sealed them inside hollow reeds — not the single bamboo of the sipapu story, but many reeds, each one large enough to hold a family.

The flood came from below, not above. The ground opened and water poured in, rising faster than anyone could climb. The reeds floated, bobbing on the surface like cattails on a pond. The people huddled inside, listening to the Third World drown beneath them.

For days they floated. The water was endless in every direction — no land, no mountains, no landmark of any kind. The people grew afraid. "We will starve," they said. "There is nothing to eat on the water."

Spider Grandmother told them to make boats from more reeds. They wove the reeds into rafts and sailed east, using the position of the sun to guide them. They stopped at islands that rose from the water — stepping-stones of rock and sand — and rested before continuing.

The Hopi Water Clan's name, Patkinyamu, means 'dwelling-on-water,' preserving the memory of this ocean voyage in their very identity.

After many days, the mountains of the Fourth World rose from the water like the backs of sleeping giants. The people climbed ashore, exhausted and sunburned, and collapsed on the rocky coast. They had nothing — no tools, no food, no shelter. Spider Grandmother taught them to make boats from the reeds they still carried, to fish with sharpened sticks, to build shelters from driftwood.

The sipapu story and the flood story are both told. Different villages emphasize different versions. But both agree on this: the people who reached the Fourth World were chosen for their goodness, and they were given a second chance.

title: The Hopi Clan Migrations
summary: Upon arriving in the Fourth World, the Hopi divided and began great migrations across the land. Led by various signs and helped by Spider Woman, clans traveled to every direction, sometimes stopping to build towns, then abandoning them to continue their migrations. They left symbols on rocks to show that Hopi had been there. Clans were named after events or signs received during their journeys. Periods of harmonious living alternated with wickedness, contention, and separation — a pattern that began in the First World. The clans traveled to the farthest extremity of the land in every direction; far to the north was the 'Back Door' (possibly the Bering land bridge), but this was closed to the Hopi, though other peoples came through it. Eventually, guided by Masauwu, the Hopi were led to their permanent home in northeastern Arizona, where Masauwu gave them the land in exchange for their stewardship and service.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis; Ekkehart Malotki, Hopi Ruin Legends
full_text:
When the Hopi first arrived in the Fourth World, they were one people — speaking one language, following one set of customs. But the land was vast, and Masauwu had given them four tablets with instructions to explore, to settle, and to remember.

The clans divided. Some went north, some south, some east, some west. They carried with them the knowledge Spider Grandmother had given them — how to plant corn, how to build houses, how to perform ceremonies. They left symbols on rocks as they traveled, marking their passage the way a bird marks its path through the sky.

Clans were named after events or signs. The Corn Clan was named because they found a field of corn growing wild. The Bear Clan was named because a bear led them to water. The Firewood Clan was named because they gathered the best firewood. Each name carried a story, and each story carried a lesson.

Periods of harmony alternated with wickedness, contention, and separation — a pattern that had begun in the First World and would repeat through every world. Some clans stopped migrating and built towns, only to abandon them when the springs dried up or the soil grew thin.

Far to the north was the Back Door — possibly the Bering land bridge — through which other peoples had entered the Fourth World. But this door was closed to the Hopi. Their path was different. Their destination was specific.

Masauwu guided them. He appeared at crossroads and on mountaintops, wearing his mask of death and life. "Go east," he told one clan. "Go south," he told another. "Go to the place where three mesas stand like prayer sticks pointing at the sky."

Eventually, the clans converged in northeastern Arizona, on the three mesas that Masauwu had promised. They built their towns — Walpi on First Mesa, Shongopavi and Oraibi on Second and Third Mesa — and planted their corn in the dry soil. The migrations were over. The Hopi were home.

But the stories of the journey are preserved in their dances, their songs, and the petroglyphs that still mark the rocks across the Southwest — a map of wandering written in stone.

title: The Kachinas Bring Agriculture
summary: In Hopi tradition, during a great drought when the people were starving, they heard singing and dancing coming from the San Francisco Peaks (Nuvatukya'ovi). Investigating, they met the Kachinas — ancestral spirits and supernatural beings who inhabit the peaks. The Kachinas returned with the Hopi to their villages and taught them agriculture, including how to plant and care for corn, beans, and squash. They also taught the Hopi their ceremonial dances and songs, which are vital for bringing rain to the arid land. For six months each year (from winter solstice to July), the Kachina spirits leave the San Francisco Peaks and live in the Hopi villages. Men who put on the masks become the Kachinas — the mask is not a costume but a face that transforms the wearer. The Niman (Homegoing) ceremony in late July marks the Kachinas' return to the mountains.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Pecina and Pecina, Hopi Kachinas (2013)
full_text:
The drought lasted twelve years. The springs dried to mud. The corn withered in the fields, its leaves curling brown in the relentless sun. Children cried from hunger, and the elders whispered that the Kachinas had abandoned them.

But the Kachinas had not abandoned them. They were watching from the San Francisco Peaks — Nuvatukya'ovi — the sacred mountains north of the villages, hidden in clouds that refused to rain.

One evening, a young girl heard singing coming from the direction of the peaks. She told her grandmother, who told the chief, who gathered the people. They listened. The singing was beautiful, rising and falling like water flowing over stones.

They followed the sound to the base of the mountains and found the Kachinas — ancestral spirits, supernatural beings who had lived in the peaks since the beginning of the Fourth World. The Kachinas agreed to return with the people to their villages.

They came in a great procession. The Kachinas wore masks of every kind — parrot and eagle, deer and bear, sun and moon. They danced in the plazas, their feet stamping the dry earth, their songs calling to the rain spirits. And the rain came.

The Kachinas taught the people agriculture — not just how to plant corn, but how to read the clouds, how to read the soil, how to know when the sun was right and when the frost was done. They taught the ceremonies that would bring rain each year — the dances, the songs, the prayers that are not merely requests but negotiations with the forces of the sky.

For six months each year, from winter solstice to July, the Kachina spirits live in the Hopi villages. Men who put on the masks do not merely represent the Kachinas — they become them. The mask is not a costume but a face that transforms the wearer into something more than human.

In late July, the Niman — the Homegoing ceremony — marks the Kachinas' return to the mountains. The people watch them go, knowing they will return when the winter solstice turns the year, bringing rain and blessings once more.

title: The Kana-a Kachinas of Sunset Crater
summary: At old Mishongnovi lived a young maiden who refused all suitors. A Kachina youth from the San Francisco Peaks courted her through magical means — traveling by rainbow — and brought her across the desert to Palotsmo (Sunset Crater), home of the Kana-a Kachinas. There she underwent tests in the kiva, surviving four nights in an icy room with the North Wind, and passed. She married the Kachina youth. But a wicked man impersonated the Kachina husband and deceived the maiden. The Kana-a Kachinas at Sunset Crater took pity on the people suffering from the consequences of this deception. They brought sweet corn and food to the Hopi villages, dancing through the streets, asking each family to leave an ear of corn in their empty storage room. When the people awoke the next morning, their storage rooms were miraculously full of corn. The Kana-a Kachinas then entered a small butte near Mishongnovi, which remains their home.
source: Edmund Nequatewa, Truth of a Hopi; Sacred-texts.com
full_text:
At old Mishongnovi, on Second Mesa, there lived a maiden who refused every suitor. She was proud and beautiful, and she wanted nothing to do with the young men of her village, who were, in her opinion, unremarkable.

One day, a Kachina youth from the San Francisco Peaks saw her and fell in love. He traveled to Mishongnovi by rainbow — stepping from one color to the next until he stood at the edge of the village. He courted her with gifts of turquoise and feathers, with songs that made the corn grow taller just by hearing them.

The maiden agreed to go with him. He led her across the desert to Palotsmo — Sunset Crater — where the Kana-a Kachinas lived in a village of red stone.

But first, she had to prove herself. The Kachinas placed her in the kiva — the ceremonial chamber — and left her there for four nights. Each night, the North Wind entered the kiva and tried to freeze her. The first night, the cold was bitter. The second night, it was unbearable. The third night, the maiden's breath turned to ice crystals. But she held firm, wrapped in the songs her mother had taught her, and the North Wind could not break her.

On the fourth night, she emerged from the kiva, transformed. The Kana-a Kachinas accepted her as one of their own. She married the youth and lived among them.

But back in Mishongnovi, a wicked man had heard of the maiden's journey. He disguised himself as the Kachina husband and deceived the people, causing harm that echoed through the village.

The Kana-a Kachinas at Sunset Crater took pity on the people suffering from this deception. They gathered sweet corn and food, and in a great procession they danced through the streets of Mishongnovi. At each house, they asked the people to leave an ear of corn in their empty storage room. When the people awoke the next morning, their storage rooms were miraculously full of corn.

The Kana-a Kachinas then entered a small butte near the village, which remains their home to this day. The people of Mishongnovi leave offerings at its base, remembering the gift of corn and the lesson that even deception cannot long obscure the truth.

title: The Ahö'li and the Kachinas of Walpi
summary: In Walpi lived an old Ahö'li Kachina with his sister, the Kachin-mana, leading her because of his age and frailty. They planted in their field south of Walpi, depositing prayer offerings at a báho shrine. Meanwhile, the Ââ'ototo, Big-Horn Kachina, and others gathered and descended the mesa, marking shrines between villages. They encountered the Cóoyoko, a dangerous being with protruding eyes, a large knife, and rattles around his body, who killed and devoured children. The Kachinas negotiated safe passage, promising Cóoyoko could destroy only the bad. The Kachinas descended to a beautiful house in the valley where they sang all night, and the next morning rain poured. By noon, the fields were filled with corn, melons, and squashes. Big-Skeleton (Wokómásauwuu), who owns the earth, met them and told them to live on top of the mesa, where Walpi eventually moved.
source: H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905)
full_text:
In Walpi, on First Mesa, an old Ahö'li Kachina lived with his sister, the Kachin-mana. He was so old and frail that his sister led him by the hand wherever he went. They planted in their field south of the mesa, and at each corner they placed a báho — a small prayer offering of woven cotton and feathers.

Meanwhile, above them in the kivas, the great Kachinas were preparing. The Ââ'ototo, Big-Horn Kachina, led a procession down the mesa, marking shrines between the villages with sacred objects.

As they descended into the valley, they encountered the Cóoyoko — a dangerous being with protruding eyes, a large knife, and rattles of bone and shell around his body. The Cóoyoko killed and devoured children who wandered too far from the village.

The Kachinas negotiated with the Cóoyoko. "Let us pass," they said. "We will bring rain to the fields. In return, you may destroy only the bad — the wicked and the cruel."

The Cóoyoko agreed. The Kachinas continued into the valley, where they found a beautiful house hidden in the cottonwood trees. They entered and sang all night — songs of rain, songs of growth, songs of the earth opening to receive the sky's gift.

By morning, rain poured from clouds that had not been there the night before. The dry arroyos filled. The fields drank deeply. By noon, the sun broke through, and the Kachinas emerged from the house to find their fields filled with corn, melons, and squashes — all growing at supernatural speed, as if the earth were making up for twelve years of drought in a single morning.

Big-Skeleton — Wokómásauwuu — who owns the earth and all that grows upon it, met the Kachinas as they climbed back toward the mesa. "You have done well," he said. "But you must live on top of the mesa, not in the valley. The valley is for growing. The mesa is for watching."

And so Walpi was built on the very top of First Mesa, where the Kachinas could look down upon their fields and the people could look up at the sky.

title: The Circle Kachina and His Wife Become Stars
summary: In Hopi tradition, a maiden grinding corn was approached by the Póngo (Circle) Kachina, who danced at various kivas around the village. She agreed to marry him and went to the Kachina kiva where many different Kachinas gathered. She prepared their food while they prepared her bridal costume. They had two children, also Circle Kachinas. The Hotóto Kachina seduced the wife away to Shongópavi. The Circle Kachina, following her tracks, took his children to the Kachina house. After four days of flute playing at Kíba, the wife emerged from the water in her bridal costume. The Flute priests declared: 'You shall always follow each other this way.' The two ran westward and are still running — they became the stars that pursue each other across the sky, Nangö'sohu, one constantly overtaking and then falling behind the other.
source: H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905)
full_text:
A maiden in the village was grinding corn in her lodge, the rhythmic sound of the metate filling the room like a heartbeat, when the Póngo — Circle Kachina — appeared at her door. He had been dancing at the kivas around the village, his round mask painted with the symbols of the four directions, his body wrapped in fine white cotton.

He danced for her — a courtship dance, his feet stamping the hard-packed floor, his arms spreading like wings. She smiled. She agreed to marry him.

She went to the Kachina kiva, where many different Kachinas gathered — Crow Mother, the Parrot Kachinas, the warrior Kachinas — all preparing for the spring dances. She cooked their food while they wove her bridal costume: a robe of white turkey feathers, a belt of turquoise beads, moccasins of soft deerskin.

They had two children, both Circle Kachinas — small, round-faced beings who danced in the plazas with their father.

But the Hotóto Kachina — a being of great charm and questionable intentions — seduced the wife away to Shongópavi, another village on Second Mesa. The Circle Kachina followed her tracks across the mesa, carrying his children on his back.

At the kiva in Shongópavi, the Flute priests played for four days. The music was so beautiful that the water spirits wept, and their tears formed a pool at the kiva's entrance. On the fourth day, the wife emerged from the water in her bridal costume, restored.

The Flute priests declared: "You shall always follow each other this way."

The two ran westward. They are still running. They became the stars that chase each other across the sky — Nangö'sohu — one constantly overtaking and then falling behind the other. In the Hopi sky, you can see them every night: two points of light, forever pursuing, forever separated, forever connected.

title: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas
summary: In Oraibi, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. North of the village at Katcínavala lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy often went to listen to the Kachinas sing. On the dance day, the Toad Boy painted his face and wore a wildcat robe. Children laughed at him and took him to an anthill because he liked ants. He ate the ants and returned to the plaza to enjoy the dance. When the children gave him red piki (paper bread) from the Kachinas, he brought it home to his mother. She was happy, and they ate it together. This story teaches about the inclusion of even the lowliest creatures in Kachina celebrations and demonstrates the Hopi value of kindness to those who are different.
source: H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905); told by Kwáyeshva of Oraíbi
full_text:
In Oraibi, on Third Mesa, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. Their masks were white as the first frost, and their songs were the songs of winter — slow, deep, resonant with the weight of snow.

North of the village, at a place called Katcínavala, lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy was small and strange — his skin bumpy, his eyes too large, his manner quiet. He liked ants. He would sit for hours watching them carry seeds across the sand, marveling at their industry.

Every day, the boy crept to the kiva and pressed his ear against the stone wall, listening to the Kachinas sing. The music moved him in ways he could not explain. His feet tapped. His hands waved. He wanted to dance.

On the day of the dance, the Toad Boy painted his face with red ochre and wore a wildcat robe over his small, bumpy body. He walked to the plaza and stood among the children.

The children laughed at him. "Look at the Toad Boy!" they cried. "He thinks he can dance!" They grabbed him and carried him to an anthill, dumping him on top of it because he liked ants.

The boy sat on the anthill and ate the ants, one by one, while the dance continued. When the Kachinas finished, they gave the children red piki — thin, paper-like bread made from blue corn. The Toad Boy received a piece. He carried it home to his mother.

She was happy. They ate it together in their small lodge, the sweet, thin bread dissolving on their tongues.

This story teaches a Hopi value that runs deeper than it appears: inclusion. Even the lowliest creature — a toad boy who eats ants — has a place in the Kachina celebrations. The dance is not for the beautiful or the strong. It is for everyone. And the gift of piki, that thin red bread, is the gift of community itself.

title: Coyote Helps Decorate the Night
summary: In this Hopi story about the origins of the night sky, the animals were decorating the darkness. Various animals placed stars and patterns in the sky, but Coyote, growing impatient with the slow, careful work, grabbed a handful of stars and threw them carelessly across the sky. This explains why some stars are scattered randomly while others form orderly patterns. Another version tells that Coyote was given the task of placing the stars but became distracted or deliberately did a poor job, resulting in the Milky Way and the chaotic scattering of stars. The story warns against impatience and the consequences of rushing sacred work.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
In the time before the stars were placed, the sky was a blank canvas of darkness, and the animals were given the task of decorating it.

The Beaver went first. He was careful and methodical, placing each star in a straight line, like the logs of a dam. The Deer followed, arranging stars in gentle arcs that mirrored the paths she walked through the forest. The Eagle placed the brightest stars in patterns that resembled wings spread against the night.

Coyote watched. He had been given the task of placing the scattered stars — the ones that did not fit into any pattern, the ones that were too small or too dim for the important constellations.

The work was slow. Each animal placed a star, then stepped back to admire it, then placed another. The night was cold and the work was tedious. Coyote grew impatient.

"This is taking too long," he said. "Let me help."

The other animals were wary, but they gave him a blanket full of stars — hundreds of them, glowing faintly like embers. Coyote grabbed the blanket and flung it into the sky.

Stars scattered in every direction. Some landed in neat rows. Others landed in clumps. Some landed alone, isolated in vast dark spaces. The careful patterns the other animals had created were disrupted, overlaid with Coyote's chaotic scatter.

The animals were angry. "You've ruined it!" the Beaver cried.

But the Creator looked at the sky and saw something the animals did not. The orderly patterns — the Big Dipper, the Hunter, the Pleiades — told stories and marked seasons. But Coyote's scattered stars filled the spaces between, creating the Milky Way and the countless faint lights that make the night sky feel infinite.

"Both are necessary," the Creator said. "Order without chaos is a cage. Chaos without order is a flood. Together, they are the sky."

And so the night remains: partly patterned, partly scattered, partly deliberate, partly accidental — like the world itself.

title: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned
summary: A Hopi tale of a boy who journeyed across the great waters and returned with knowledge and power. The boy's curiosity led him to leave his village and travel east toward the rising sun. He encountered various supernatural beings and overcame trials, including crossing a body of water that no Hopi had crossed before. Guided by Spider Grandmother, he learned sacred songs and ceremonies from the spirits on the other side. When he returned to his people, he brought new ceremonies, dance forms, and agricultural knowledge that benefited the Hopi. The story reflects the Hopi belief that spiritual power and knowledge can be gained through journeys to sacred places and that those who venture forth with pure hearts return to enrich the community.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
The boy's name has been lost, which is fitting, because the story is not about who he was but about what he found. He lived in a village on the mesas, a quiet boy with restless feet and a mind that wandered beyond the horizon.

One morning, he left. He told no one where he was going. He walked east, toward the rising sun, carrying nothing but a water gourd and a piece of dried corn.

He walked for many days. The mesas gave way to valleys, the valleys to plains, the plains to mountains he had never seen. He crossed rivers too wide to see the other side and climbed passes where the air was thin enough to make him dizzy.

Guided by Spider Grandmother — who appeared to him as an old woman sitting by a fire — he found his way to a body of water so vast it might have been the edge of the world. On the other side, he could see mountains glowing with a light that was not sunlight.

Spider Grandmother taught him to build a boat from reeds and to navigate by the stars. He crossed the water and found a land where spirits lived in houses of cloud and spoke in songs. They taught him sacred ceremonies — dances that brought rain, songs that healed the sick, prayers that opened the way between the living and the dead.

He stayed for one year, learning everything the spirits could teach. When he returned to his people, he brought new dances, new songs, and new knowledge of agriculture — how to read the stars to know when to plant, how to read the clouds to know when rain was coming.

The people benefited from his journey. The corn grew taller. The children grew stronger. The ceremonies became richer.

The boy — for he was still a boy, though his eyes were old — never spoke about where he had been. But sometimes, at night, he would sit outside his lodge and look east, toward the water he had crossed, and the people knew that the knowledge he carried had come from a place beyond the ordinary world.

title: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits
summary: Coyote and Bull Snake were friends who decided to visit each other's homes. Coyote visited Bull Snake first and found his burrow beautiful and comfortable. Bull Snake then visited Coyote's den. During the visit, Coyote played a trick on Bull Snake, or vice versa, depending on the version. The story humorously explores the nature of friendship across differences, the expectations of hospitality, and the consequences of deception between friends. It also incorporates elements of Hopi social values, including proper guest behavior and the responsibilities of hosts. The story ends with the two friends parting ways, each having learned something about trust and respect for different ways of living.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
Coyote and Bull Snake were friends — an unlikely pair, for Coyote was loud and restless while Bull Snake was quiet and still. But friendship, like rain, falls where it will.

Coyote visited Bull Snake first. He found the burrow beautiful — cool and dark, with walls that glowed faintly with embedded crystals. Bull Snake offered Coyote the best sleeping spot, the one near the back where the air was warmest.

"Now you must visit my den," Coyote said.

Bull Snake agreed and traveled to Coyote's home — a hollow under a rock, messy with old bones and scattered fur. Bull Snake was polite, though the smell was terrible.

During the visit, Coyote decided to play a trick. He told Bull Snake that the greatest honor in his den was to sleep in the deepest corner, where the air was thinnest. Bull Snake, trusting his friend, slithered into the deepest part of the den — and found himself stuck, his thick body wedged between two rocks.

Coyote laughed. "I've caught a snake!" he cried.

But Bull Snake did not laugh. He spoke quietly: "A friend who tricks his guest is no friend at all."

Coyote's laughter died. He helped Bull Snake out of the crevice, cleaning the dirt from his scales with his own paws. "I am sorry," he said, and for once, he meant it.

Bull Snake returned to his own burrow, and Coyote did not visit for a long time. When he finally did, he brought a gift — a fine piece of turquoise, smoothed by the river. Bull Snake accepted it, and the friendship resumed, though it was changed.

The story teaches Hopi values about hospitality and the responsibilities of hosts. A guest must be treated with respect, and a host who betrays that trust loses something that cannot be easily regained.

title: Why the Salt is Far Away
summary: A Hopi legend explaining why the Hopi must travel long distances to obtain salt. Long ago, salt was close to the Hopi villages. But a woman or a group of people violated a taboo involving salt — either by being wasteful, disrespectful, or by using salt improperly during a ceremony. The Salt Woman (or salt spirits) became angry and moved the salt deposits far away, to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations. Ever since, the Hopi have had to undertake long, dangerous journeys to gather salt, a sacred substance used in ceremonies and daily life. The story teaches respect for natural resources and the consequences of taking blessings for granted.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993); various Hopi oral traditions
full_text:
Salt was once close to the Hopi villages. It lay in deposits along the riverbanks, white and crystalline, easy to gather. The people used it freely — sprinkling it on corn, preserving meat, marking the boundaries of their fields. They did not think about where it came from or how blessed they were to have it.

Salt Woman saw this. She was a spirit — old and powerful, her body made of the same white crystal as the salt itself. She lived in the deposits, and the people's carelessness wounded her. They wasted salt. They used it in ways that were not sacred. They forgot to give thanks.

One night, Salt Woman packed her belongings — which were also salt — and walked away from the villages. She walked south, toward the Grand Canyon, where the river carved through layers of ancient rock. She walked to other places too — to distant salt flats and underground deposits.

When the people went to gather salt the next morning, the riverbanks were bare. The deposits were gone. They searched everywhere and found nothing.

A hunter tracked Salt Woman's footprints to the Grand Canyon. There he found her, sitting on a ledge overlooking the river. "Come back," he begged. "We need the salt."

Salt Woman looked at him with eyes like white stone. "You forgot to give thanks," she said. "You forgot that the salt is a gift, not a right. If you want salt, you will have to come and get it — the long way, the hard way, so that you remember."

The hunter returned to his people with Salt Woman's words. And so the Hopi began their long journeys to gather salt — traveling for days to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations, carrying the salt back on their backs.

The journey itself became sacred. The people sang songs as they walked. They left offerings at every spring and shrine along the way. And when they returned with the white crystals, they gave thanks — not just for the salt, but for the reminder that blessings must never be taken for granted.

title: The Journey to the Land of the Dead
summary: In Hopi tradition, the journey to the land of the dead begins at the sipapu in the Grand Canyon. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, to the land of the ancestors. Along the way, the spirit encounters various challenges and must have the proper knowledge, gained through ceremonial instruction during life, to pass safely. The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas who determine its fate. Good souls pass into a land of plenty, while those who lived badly face difficulties. The dead eventually become cloud people who can bring rain to their living descendants. The spirits of the dead are associated with the Kachinas and reside at the San Francisco Peaks. This cycle of life, death, and return as rain-giving spirits reinforces the Hopi connection between proper living, ceremonial participation, and the well-being of the community.
source: Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis; H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905)
full_text:
When a Hopi dies, the journey begins at the sipapu — the opening in the Grand Canyon where the people first entered the Fourth World. The spirit descends through this passage, back through the layers of the earth, following the path that the ancestors once climbed.

But the journey is not a straight descent. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, moving through a landscape that is both familiar and strange — a shadow version of the living world, where the rivers flow backward and the mountains lean in directions that make no sense.

Along the way, the spirit encounters challenges. There are crossings where the bridge is made of a single hair, and the spirit must be light enough to walk it. There are gates guarded by spirits who ask questions that only the properly instructed can answer. There are tests of character — moments where the spirit must prove that it lived well, that it honored the ceremonies, that it treated others with respect.

The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas. Those who lived well pass into a land of plenty — a world like the Fourth World but better, where the corn grows tall and the water flows clear. Those who lived badly face difficulties — not punishment, but the consequences of their choices, a world shaped by their own failures.

The dead eventually become cloud people. They rise from the land of the dead into the sky, where they join the Kachinas at the San Francisco Peaks. From there, they can bring rain to their living descendants. The dead are not gone — they are transformed, becoming part of the forces that sustain the living world.

This is why the Hopi perform ceremonies for the dead. They pray not for the dead to return, but for the dead to find their place among the cloud people, where they can fulfill their final duty: bringing rain to the fields that feed their children and their children's children.

title: Mockingbird Gives Out the Calls
summary: In this Hopi story, Mockingbird was responsible for distributing the languages and calls among all the peoples of the world. During the migrations after the emergence into the Fourth World, the people were all speaking the same language. Mockingbird called the people together and assigned different languages and dialects to different groups, effectively creating the diversity of tribes and nations. He gave various bird species their distinctive calls as well. According to some versions, Mockingbird received this task from Spider Grandmother or the Kachinas, and his imitative ability was used to create the range of human languages. The story explains why Mockingbird can mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
In the time after the emergence, when the people first spread across the Fourth World, they all spoke the same language. Every clan, every village, every family — the words flowed between them like water between connected springs.

Mockingbird saw this and was troubled. "The world is too large for one language," he said. "If everyone speaks the same words, they will never be truly different. They will never have their own songs, their own stories, their own way of seeing the world."

Mockingbird had been given a special gift by the Creator: the ability to imitate any sound, any voice, any song. He could sound like a hawk or a frog, like wind in the pines or water over stones. This gift made him the natural choice for what needed to be done.

He called the people together at the base of a great mesa. They gathered in hundreds, their voices rising in a single chorus of the common tongue. Mockingbird perched on a rock above them and began to sing.

He sang the song of the Hawk, and the people of the north spoke in sharp, clipped tones. He sang the song of the Frog, and the people of the south spoke in deep, resonant voices. He sang the song of the Wind, and the people of the east spoke in words that moved quickly, like grass bending in a breeze. He sang the song of the River, and the people of the west spoke in words that flowed slowly and steadily.

He gave each group its own language, its own dialect, its own way of forming words. The people tried to speak to each other and found they could not understand. They laughed. They wept. They gestured. And slowly, they learned to communicate through other means — through sign language, through shared work, through the universal language of ceremony.

Mockingbird also gave the bird species their distinctive calls. The hawk's cry, the owl's hoot, the sparrow's chirp — all are fragments of the languages Mockingbird distributed.

This is why Mockingbird can still mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth. It is not a curse but a gift — the gift of difference, of perspective, of the understanding that the world is too vast to be spoken in a single voice.

title: Sikakokuh and the Hunting Dog
summary: A Hopi story about a boy named Sikakokuh who had a remarkable hunting dog. The dog was no ordinary animal but possessed spiritual power, able to track game without fail and communicate with its master. Sikakokuh's success as a hunter made others jealous. Through the dog's guidance, Sikakokuh learned the proper rituals for hunting, including prayers and offerings to the spirits of the animals he killed. When enemies or jealous rivals tried to harm the dog, supernatural forces protected both boy and animal. The story teaches the sacred relationship between humans and animals, the importance of gratitude, and the proper conduct of hunters who must respect the spirits of the animals they take.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
Sikakokuh was a boy of the Hopi villages who possessed a hunting dog unlike any other — a creature born with eyes the color of river stones and a spirit that seemed to know things no animal should know. Where other dogs chased rabbits blindly through the mesas, Sikakokuh's dog would pause at the edge of the wash, lift its nose, and point toward exactly where a deer would be standing three valleys away.

The other hunters noticed. They whispered. "How does the boy find game every time?" jealousy poisoned their words like stagnant water. Some began to scheme against the dog, for they believed it carried bad spirits.

But the dog was no ordinary animal. In dreams, it spoke to Sikakokuh in a voice like wind through canyon walls. "When you hunt, you must first offer cornmeal to the earth. You must speak to the spirit of the animal before you draw your bow. If you take without asking, the game will hide from your people forever."

Sikakokuh followed every instruction. He scattered cornmeal at the four directions. He whispered prayers before each hunt. And the deer came willingly, walking toward his arrow as if offering themselves.

One night, a jealous hunter tried to poison the dog with tainted meat. But the spirits of the mountain — the Gahe — intervened. They appeared as masked dancers in the moonlight, their wooden headdresses scraping the stars, and they drove the wicked hunter away into the desert where he wandered for three days without water.

When the hunter returned, broken and repentant, Sikakokuh shared his harvest with him. The dog sat beside them, watching with eyes that held the memory of every hunt, every prayer, every life given so the people might eat.

"The dog is our teacher," Sikakokuh told the village elders. "It shows us that hunting is not conquest. It is conversation."

The story spread through the Hopi villages and became part of the teachings given to young hunters — a reminder that the sacred relationship between human and animal is built on respect, gratitude, and the proper conduct of ceremony.

title: The Iatiku and Nautsiti Creation (Acoma Pueblo)
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation myth, two sisters named Iatiku (Life Bringer) and Nautsiti (Full Basket) emerged from the underworld through a sacred place called Shipapu, guided by Tsichtinako (Thought Woman). They were given two baskets containing seeds, animal figurines, and sacred objects. Tsichtinako instructed them to pray to the Sun (Uchtsiti), their father, who had created the world from a clot of his own blood. The sisters created the mountains, directions, plants, and animals. Iatiku created the Corn Mother and the Kachinas. Nautsiti introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo. The sisters became the mothers of the Acoma people, with Iatiku's children becoming the Pueblo clans. The story explains the origins of ceremonies, clans, and the relationship between the people, the land, and the spirits.
source: Edward Proctor Hunt, The Origin Myth of Acoma Pueblo (1928); Peter Nabokov edition (2015)
full_text:
Before the world had shape, there was only Shipapu — a dark opening in the earth through which the first light would eventually shine.
