The canoe is fast and unsinkable, cutting through the waves like a blade, and the belt is unbreakable, turning aside arrows, spears, and even the blows of supernatural beings.

The beach mineral mica was believed to be the scales of the Sisiutl and was incorporated into ceremonial traditions. Warriors wore mica on their armor, believing it would protect them from the serpent's glance and grant them its power.

The Sisiutl plays a dual role as both a terrifying monster and a powerful helper to ancestors who earned its favor. It is not simply evil — it is powerful, and power, like fire, can warm or burn depending on how it is used.

title: Komokwa the Undersea Chief (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Komokwa (also known as Qomoqua or Copper-Maker) is the powerful chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He lives in a magnificent copper house beneath the ocean, where he controls all the wealth of the sea, including seals, sea lions, salmon, and the precious copper that gives him his name. Komokwa appears as a figure with a large, bulbous head covered in feathers or hair, often depicted with a wide mouth and protruding tongue. He sometimes takes the form of a sea monster or appears riding a Sisiutl canoe. Humans who visit his underwater kingdom must undergo dangerous trials. In some stories, a person who drowns is taken to Komokwa's house and may return with great wealth and supernatural power. Komokwa is both feared and respected; he is a generous giver of wealth to those who treat him properly but also a dangerous being who can drown anyone who disrespects the sea.
source: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Ethnography; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
full_text:
Komokwa, also known as Qomoqua or Copper-Maker, is the powerful chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He lives in a magnificent copper house beneath the ocean, where he controls all the wealth of the sea, including seals, sea lions, salmon, and the precious copper that gives him his name.

Komokwa appears as a figure with a large, bulbous head covered in feathers or hair, often depicted with a wide mouth and protruding tongue. He sometimes takes the form of a sea monster or appears riding a Sisiutl canoe — a vessel that cuts through the water like a blade, its twin heads snapping at the waves.

Humans who visit his underwater kingdom must undergo dangerous trials. They must dive to the bottom of the ocean, holding their breath, swimming through the darkness where the pressure crushes the chest and the cold numbs the limbs. They must pass through the gates of Komokwa's house, guarded by supernatural beings who test their courage and their worth.

In some stories, a person who drowns is taken to Komokwa's house and may return with great wealth and supernatural power. The drowned person is not dead — they are transformed, remade by the undersea chief, returned to the surface as a being of power.

Komokwa is both feared and respected; he is a generous giver of wealth to those who treat him properly but also a dangerous being who can drown anyone who disrespects the sea. The copper he controls is the most valuable material in Kwakwaka'wakw culture — a symbol of wealth, power, and prestige. To receive copper from Komokwa is to receive the highest possible gift, and to give copper is to make the highest possible sacrifice.

The undersea kingdom of Komokwa is a mirror of the human world — a place with chiefs and commoners, with wealth and poverty, with order and chaos. But it is also different: more beautiful, more dangerous, and more permanent than the fleeting world of humans.

title: The Cannibal Woman Society (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Long ago when totemic beings walked the earth, there was Dzunukwa (Cannibal Woman), a gigantic female being with great wealth and powerful magic who ate people. The other beings became alarmed and decided only Raven could stop her. Raven flew to the North End of the World and recruited a flock of fearsome Cannibal Birds, becoming their leader. He returned with his flock to the great forest where Dzunukwa lived, and they danced and sang her praises. When the dance ended, Dzunukwa found herself bound by powerful magic and could no longer eat flesh — the only things she could eat were nuggets of native copper. This story establishes the origin of the Hamatsa (Cannibal Woman) Society, the most important secret society in Kwakwaka'wakw culture. The society's winter ceremonies reenact the capturing and taming of the cannibal spirit, transforming its destructive power into constructive social and spiritual energy for the community.
source: Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition; Charles M. Nelson
full_text:
Long ago when totemic beings walked the earth, there was Dzunukwa — Cannibal Woman — a gigantic female being with great wealth and powerful magic who ate people. She was enormous, taller than the tallest cedar, with arms that could reach across a river and a mouth that could swallow a canoe.

The other beings became alarmed. Dzunukwa was eating too many of them, and her appetite was growing. She was not satisfied with one person at a time — she wanted more, always more, and her hunger was insatiable. They decided only Raven could stop her.

Raven flew to the North End of the World and recruited a flock of fearsome Cannibal Birds — creatures with iron beaks and talons that could tear through cedar bark. He became their leader, and they followed him south, their wings beating the air into a frenzy.

He returned with his flock to the great forest where Dzunukwa lived, and they danced and sang her praises. The dance was elaborate — a ceremony of movement and sound that called the cannibal spirit and bound it with magic. When the dance ended, Dzunukwa found herself bound by powerful magic and could no longer eat flesh — the only things she could eat were nuggets of native copper.

This story establishes the origin of the Hamatsa — the Cannibal Woman — Society, the most important secret society in Kwakwaka'wakw culture. The society's winter ceremonies reenact the capturing and taming of the cannibal spirit, transforming its destructive power into constructive social and spiritual energy for the community.

The ceremony is not simply a performance — it is a renewal of the ancient agreement between the cannibal spirits and the human community. Each year, the spirits are bound again, and each year, the community is strengthened by the process.

title: Bukwus the Wild Man of the Woods (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests and is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure. Bukwus roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the forest with promises of food. He is particularly dangerous because he appears as a starving, pitiful figure who begs for help, but anyone who follows him becomes lost forever and joins his ghostly company. Unlike D'Sonoqua, who is more easily outwitted, Bukwus is treacherous and deceptive. However, like D'Sonoqua, he is also associated with great wealth and can bestow supernatural powers upon those who manage to survive an encounter with him. Bukwus appears in both the T'seka (Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies) and the Tła'sala (Peace Dances), where dancers wear masks depicting his gaunt, haunted features.
source: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Ethnography; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
full_text:
Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests, in the places where the trees grow so thick that the sky is invisible and the ground is carpeted with moss so deep that a person can sink to their knees.

Bukwus is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure — the unfortunates who perished in the wilderness, whose bodies were never found, whose names were never spoken. Their spirits lingered in the forest, and Bukwus was their keeper, their warden, their king.

He roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the forest with promises of food. The voice is thin and reedy, like the sound of wind through dead branches, and it carries a melody that is almost beautiful but ultimately wrong — a melody that promises warmth but delivers cold, that promises fullness but delivers emptiness.

He is particularly dangerous because he appears as a starving, pitiful figure who begs for help. He stands at the edge of the trail, his body gaunt, his eyes hollow, his arms extended in a gesture of need. Anyone who follows him becomes lost forever and joins his ghostly company.

Unlike D'Sonoqua, who is more easily outwitted, Bukwus is treacherous and deceptive. He does not simply grab his victims — he lures them, guides them, leads them deeper and deeper into the forest until they cannot find their way out. The trail disappears. The landmarks change. The trees look the same in every direction. And Bukwus walks ahead, his hollow voice calling, his gaunt figure visible for just a moment before it vanishes into the shadows.

However, like D'Sonoqua, he is also associated with great wealth and can bestow supernatural powers upon those who manage to survive an encounter with him. A person who escapes Bukwus gains knowledge of the forest that no other human possesses — the location of hidden springs, the trails of supernatural beings, the songs that open the doors between worlds.

Bukwus appears in both the T'seka — Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies — and the Tla'sala — Peace Dances — where dancers wear masks depicting his gaunt, haunted features.

title: Changer and the Creation of the World (Coast Salish)
summary: In Coast Salish tradition, dukʷibəɬ the Changer (also known as Xe'las or Xelas) walked the earth when the world was not yet as it is today. Sometimes he appeared as a brilliant light from the East, sometimes as a young man, sometimes as several young men, and sometimes as an invisible old person who knew everything. The Changer went everywhere, preparing the world for the First People who were yet to come. He transformed inappropriate things into useful ones: he turned rocks that beat people over the head into hammers, sticks that struck people into fish spears, and dangerous beings into animals, birds, and landscape features. The Changer also sent a flood to cleanse the earth when things went wrong. All living things were destroyed except one woman and one dog, who fled to the top of Tacobud (Mount Rainier). From them, the next race of people was born. The Changer's work established the Coast Salish understanding of the world as a place shaped by a powerful transformer who continues to watch over the land and its people.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; Hibulb Cultural Center; Franz Boas; Brian Thom, Transformer Stories
full_text:
In the time before the First People walked the earth, when the world was still raw and unfinished — a place of jagged rock, tangled forest, and water that did not know its own edges — there walked a being of immense power and quiet purpose. The Coast Salish called him dukʷibəɬ the Changer, though he was known by other names as well: Xe'las, Xelas, the Transformer. He came from the East, and sometimes he appeared as a brilliant light moving across the sky, and sometimes as a young man with clear eyes and steady hands, and sometimes as several young men walking together, and sometimes as an invisible old person who saw everything and said nothing.

The Changer walked everywhere. He climbed the ridges where the cedar trees grew so tall their crowns vanished into cloud. He waded the rivers where salmon ran in silver millions. He crossed the valleys where the brush grew so thick that a man could not push through without bleeding. He saw what the world was, and he saw what it needed to become.

The world, in those early days, was full of things that were wrong. There were rocks that sat by the trail and waited for travelers to pass, then rose up and beat them over the head. There were sticks leaning against trees that lashed out at anyone who touched them. There were beings — neither human nor animal, but something in between — that preyed on the defenseless, that spread disease, that brought confusion and sorrow wherever they walked.

The Changer stopped these things. He did not destroy them — the Changer was not a destroyer — but he changed them. He picked up the murderous rocks and declared, "From now on, you shall be hammers. The people shall use you to shape their world." And the rocks became hammers, useful and obedient. He took the striking sticks and broke them in two. "You shall be fish spears," he said, "and the people shall feed themselves with your aid." And the sticks became spears, and the people fished.

The dangerous beings he met — the ones that spread sickness, the ones that lured travelers to their deaths — he changed as well. Some he turned into animals: deer, bear, eagle, the small creatures of the forest. Some he turned into birds that sang warnings from the treetops. Some he turned into landscape features — a boulder here, a ridge there, a waterfall cascading down a cliff face — so that they could never harm anyone again, but would stand as reminders of what the world had been before the Changer made it right.

Every rock, every stream, every bend in the river, every distinctive feature of the land — the Coast Salish understood these as the marks of the Changer's work. The landscape was his story, written in stone and water and the shapes of mountains.

But the Changer's work was not finished when the land was made safe. He sent a flood — a great cleansing water that rose from the rivers and lakes and covered the earth, washing away everything that remained of the old, broken world. Everything living perished in that flood — every animal, every plant, every creature that breathed. All were destroyed.

Almost all. One woman survived. She fled to the top of Tacobud — the great mountain that the people would later call Mount Rainier — and there she crouched on the highest peak, wrapped in her cedar bark cloak, watching the waters rise around her. With her was a dog — a small, loyal creature who had followed her without hesitation when she ran.

On the mountaintop, with the flood waters lapping at the rocks below and the sky dark with rain, the woman and the dog waited. And when the waters receded and the earth appeared again, clean and new, the woman descended from Tacobud and walked upon a world remade. From her and from the dog, the next race of people was born — the ancestors of the Coast Salish, who would come to know every stone and stream of the land the Changer had prepared for them.

The Changer's work established the Coast Salish understanding of the world as a place shaped by a powerful transformer who continues to watch over the land and its people. To this day, the mountains, the rivers, the distinctive rocks and trees of Coast Salish territory are understood not as random features of nature but as the deliberate work of dukʷibəɬ — a permanent record of transformation, a landscape that teaches, and a world that was made, not given.

title: Crane and Changer (Coast Salish)
summary: As told by Snoqualmie Charlie, this story recounts how dukʷibəɬ the Changer came upon a man with very long legs standing by the shore, getting hit over the head by rocks. The Changer asked what he was doing, and the man explained he was trying to get food but the rocks kept hurting him. The Changer took the rocks, declared they would be hammers for the people, and knocked them together, transforming them into useful tools. Then the long-legged man picked up a stick to use as a fish spear, but it too hit him over the head. The Changer took the stick, broke it in two, and declared they would be fish spears. He gave the transformed items to the man and walked away, continuing his journey of preparing the world. The long-legged man was transformed into the Crane, who to this day stands on long legs at the water's edge, using his beak as a fish spear. This is one of many stories showing how the Changer shaped the world by transforming flawed ancestors into the animals and birds we know today.
source: Hibulb Cultural Center; Snoqualmie Charlie oral tradition
full_text:
As Snoqualmie Charlie told it, the story began on a stretch of shoreline where the water met the land in a tangle of driftwood and tidal pools. The Changer — dukʷibəɬ — was walking along the beach, as he often did, looking at the world and deciding what needed to change.

He came upon a man with very long legs standing at the water's edge. The man was large and awkward, his body stretched tall on limbs too thin for his frame, and he stood there getting hit over the head by rocks.

The Changer watched for a moment, then spoke. "What are you doing here?"

The long-legged man turned, blood trickling from a cut on his scalp where a rock had struck him. "I am trying to get food," he said, gesturing at the water. "But these rocks — they keep hitting me over the head."

The Changer looked at the rocks. They were the same sort of murderous stones he had encountered throughout his travels — the ones that sat by the trail and struck at passersby. But here they were rolling in with the tide, striking at anyone who stood at the water's edge.

"Give them to me," the Changer said.

The long-legged man handed over the rocks, and the Changer held them in his hands. He examined them — their weight, their shape, their sharp edges. Then he struck them together, once, twice, and the sound that came from their meeting was not the dull crack of stone on stone but a clear, ringing note, like a bell.

"From now on," the Changer declared, "you shall be hammers for the people. They shall use you to build their houses, shape their tools, and carve their canoes." And the rocks were changed. They were no longer the kind that struck at people's heads; they were the kind that fit into a hand and did useful work.

The long-legged man picked up a stick from the beach, ready to use it as a fish spear. He waded into the shallows, aimed at a shadow moving beneath the surface, and thrust — but the stick twisted in his hands and struck him across the face.

"This, too, attacks me," he said, holding his bruised cheek.

The Changer took the stick, broke it in two, and declared, "From now on, you shall be fish spears for the people. They shall use you to feed their families." And the stick became a proper spear — balanced, sharp, useful.

The Changer gave the transformed items back to the long-legged man and walked on, continuing his journey along the shore and into the forest, looking for the next thing that needed to be made right.

But the long-legged man did not remain a man. The Changer's touch had changed him as well. His body compressed and reshaped, his skin grew feathers, his arms became wings, and his long legs remained — but now they were the legs of a wading bird, thin and elegant, perfectly suited for standing at the water's edge.

He became the Crane.

To this day, the Crane stands on long legs at the water's edge, his body poised with a kind of patient dignity, using his sharp beak — the remnant of that first fish spear — to catch fish in the shallows. He is one of the Changer's works, a living record of the day the world was made right.

This is one of many stories showing how the Changer shaped the world by transforming flawed ancestors into the animals and birds we know today. The Coast Salish understood that every creature carried within it the memory of what it had once been — and the purpose the Changer had given it. The Crane was once a man who could not feed himself. Now he feeds himself effortlessly, standing in the place where water meets land, patient and precise, doing what the Changer made him to do.

title: Qals (Mink) and the Transformations (Coast Salish)
summary: Qals (Mink) is a major trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly in the Fraser River region. In the longest and most important story told by George StsE'lis to Franz Boas, Qals shapes the world through his encounters with various flawed ancestors. Mink tricked a chief's daughter into sleeping with him, producing a human boy named T'qulä'tca, who became the ancestor of the Ts'uwä'l people. Qals encountered numerous beings who needed correction: he transformed a toothed-vagina woman named LEqyiles who bit off Mink's hand into stone on the Harrison River; he changed a one-legged man into stone at StsE'lis; and he transformed whole villages of people who opposed him into animals, rocks, and landmarks. The Qals cycle demonstrates the Coast Salish concept of transformation as a world-ordering force. Everything in the landscape has a story behind it — every rock, every mountain, every bend in the river — recording where Qals walked and changed the world.
source: Franz Boas texts from StsE'lis; Brian Thom, Transformer Stories
full_text:
Qals — Mink — is a figure of contradictions. In the stories told along the Fraser River, passed down through generations of Coast Salish storytellers and recorded by Franz Boas from the lips of George StsE'lis, Mink is a trickster, a transformer, a creator, and a fool. He reshapes the world through his encounters with flawed beings, and in doing so, he creates the landscape that the Coast Salish call home.

The longest and most important of the Mink stories tells of his journey up the Fraser River, encountering one strange being after another and transforming each into something new.

It began when Mink tricked a chief's daughter into sleeping with him. This was typical of Mink — he was vain, lustful, and utterly without shame. From their union came a boy named T'qulə'tca, who grew up to become the ancestor of the Ts'uwə'l people. The chief was furious when he discovered what Mink had done, but Mink had already vanished upriver, leaving chaos in his wake.

Near the Harrison River, Mink encountered a woman named LEqyiles — a terrifying creature with a vagina full of teeth. Men who lay with her lost their organs, and some lost their lives. Mink, driven by his usual appetites, approached her anyway. When she bit off his hand, he grabbed her by the hair and transformed her into a rock formation that still stands at the Harrison River — a jagged outcropping that fishermen pass with respect and a wide berth.

At StsE'lis, Mink met a one-legged man who hopped along the shore, gathering shellfish. The man was annoying — he blocked the path, he talked too much, he asked questions that had no answers. Mink grew impatient and turned him to stone as well. That rock, too, can still be seen.

Further upriver, Mink encountered entire villages of people who opposed him — who challenged his right to pass through their territories, who questioned his authority, who made the mistake of treating him as an equal rather than as a being of supernatural power. Mink transformed them all. Some became animals — deer, bear, the small creatures of the forest. Some became rocks, or islands, or bends in the river. The landscape of the Fraser River valley, the Coast Salish understood, was Mink's canvas, and every distinctive feature was a record of his passing.

But Mink was not all power and transformation. He was also foolish, vain, and frequently outwitted by beings he considered inferior. In one story, he tried to steal fire from a chief who kept it hidden in a box. In another, he boasted of his sexual prowess to a group of women who laughed at him. In yet another, he fell in love with a woman who turned out to be a bear in disguise, and he barely escaped with his life.

The Qals cycle demonstrates the Coast Salish concept of transformation as a world-ordering force. Everything in the landscape has a story behind it — every rock, every mountain, every bend in the river — recording where Qals walked and changed the world. But the stories also carry a warning: even the most powerful being can be brought low by vanity, lust, and the refusal to listen. Mink created the world the Coast Salish live in, but he created it imperfectly, just as he himself was imperfect, and the traces of his mistakes are as visible in the landscape as the traces of his power.

title: The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things (Coast Salish)
summary: The Coast Salish people of the Olympic Peninsula tell of Ho-ho-e-ap-bess, the Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things, who were the brothers of the Sun and the Moon. When the world was very young, there were no people, birds, or animals — only grass and sand and creatures that were neither animal nor human. The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things came to earth to make it ready for a new race of people. They called all the creatures to them and transformed them: a thief became Seal, with shortened arms and tied legs so he had to catch his own fish; a creature with a long fishing spear and a white cape became Great Blue Heron, his spear becoming his bill and his cape becoming white neck feathers; a huge appetite couple became Raven and Crow, given strong beaks to tear food; Bluejay's uncooperative son became Mink, living on land and eating fish from the shore. They also created the yew tree to provide tough wood for bows. This cycle explains the origins of all Pacific Northwest animals through transformation.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; Ella E. Clark, Indian Legends of the Pacific Northwest
full_text:
When the world was very young — so young that the mountains had not yet decided where to stand and the rivers had not yet chosen their courses — there were no people, no birds, no animals. There was only grass and sand and a few strange creatures that were neither animal nor human, beings without form or purpose, wandering the earth in confusion.

Then the Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things came. Their names were Ho-ho-e-ap-bess, and they were brothers of the Sun and the Moon — beings of immense power who had lived in the sky world since before the earth was made. They came to earth to prepare it for a new race of people, and they brought with them the authority to transform everything they found.

The Two-Men were tall and radiant, their skin shining with the light of the sky world from which they had descended. They walked the earth with purpose, surveying the landscape, testing the rivers, feeling the weight of the mountains. And everywhere they went, they found beings that needed to be changed.

They called all the creatures to them — the strange, half-formed beings that wandered the earth without shape or name — and they began to transform them.

There was a creature that stole from others, taking food and tools and precious things whenever no one was looking. The Two-Men caught it and changed it. They shortened its arms and tied its legs together so that it could no longer grasp or run. "You shall be Seal," they said. "You shall live in the water and catch your own fish, and the people shall hunt you for food and clothing." And the thief became Seal, adapted to a life of honest labor in the sea.

There was a creature with a long fishing spear and a white cape who stood at the water's edge, motionless for hours. The Two-Men took the spear and placed it on the creature's face, where it became a long, sharp bill. They took the cape and wrapped it around the creature's neck, where it became a ruff of white feathers. "You shall be the Great Blue Heron," they said. "You shall stand in the shallows and catch fish with your bill, and the people shall admire your patience and grace." And the creature became Heron, still standing at the water's edge, still patient, still motionless for hours.

There was a couple with a huge appetite who ate everything in sight — berries, roots, shellfish, insects — and left nothing for anyone else. The Two-Men gave them strong beaks to tear their food and dark feathers to keep them warm in winter. "You shall be Raven and Crow," they said. "You shall eat what the people cannot eat, and you shall clean the land of what is dead." And the greedy couple became birds, useful in their gluttony.

There was a creature that refused to cooperate with anyone, that hoarded its food and refused to share, that snapped at anyone who came near. The Two-Men changed it into Mink — small, fierce, independent, living on land but eating fish from the shore. "You shall be alone," they said, "as you wished to be." And Mink became the solitary hunter that it is today.

The Two-Men also created the yew tree — a tree of extraordinary toughness and flexibility, whose wood could be bent without breaking. They made it for the people who would come later, so that they could fashion bows and hunt the animals the Two-Men had made.

This cycle explains the origins of all Pacific Northwest animals through transformation. The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things took the chaos of the unfinished world and gave it shape, purpose, and order. Every creature they created carries within it the memory of what it once was — a flawed, half-formed being that the Two-Men corrected and set right. The animals of the Pacific Northwest are not random; they are the deliberate works of two powerful beings who walked the earth before the First People and prepared it for their coming.

title: Raven Steals the Sun (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: In the Nuu-chah-nulth version of this foundational myth, there was a time before sunlight when light was kept securely in a box guarded by a great chief sometimes called the Old Fisherman. Raven wanted this light and attempted various methods to release it. He transformed himself into a floating leaf that ended up in the teacup of the great chief's daughter. She accidentally ate the leaf and in due time gave birth to Son of Raven, who was actually Raven reborn. The child was doted upon by the chief, his grandfather. Son of Raven begged to see the box of light, and after persistent pleading, the chief relented and opened the box, releasing the light. Son of Raven immediately transformed back into Raven, seized the light, and flew high into the sky. He placed the light in the sky, creating the sun that shines down on all. This myth establishes Raven as the Nuu-chah-nulth's primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; The Canadian Encyclopedia
full_text:
In the time before sunlight, when the world lay in darkness and the people stumbled through their days half-blind, light existed — but it was hoarded. A great chief, sometimes called the Old Fisherman, kept all the light of the universe locked in a nested set of five boxes, each smaller than the last, each more tightly sealed. The chief guarded his treasure jealously, letting no light escape, keeping the world in shadow.

Raven wanted that light. Not for altruistic reasons — Raven was never altruistic — but because he was tired of the dark. He wanted to see where he was walking. He wanted to find the salmon streams. He wanted to examine the faces of the people he tricked. Darkness was inconvenient for a trickster.

So Raven devised a plan — the kind of plan that only Raven could devise, involving deception, manipulation, and the exploitation of a grandfather's love.

Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle — tiny, green, nearly invisible — and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came each morning to draw water. The daughter filled her cedar bucket, carried it home, and poured it into the family's drinking vessel. The needle floated on the surface, glinting in the dim light.

When the daughter drank, she swallowed the needle. And in time, as such things happen in the stories of the beginning, she gave birth to a child — a boy with dark eyes and a cry like a raven's call. The old chief, her father, was overjoyed. He had no grandchildren, and this child was precious to him beyond measure.

The child grew with supernatural speed, and the chief doted on him, giving him everything he asked for. And what the child asked for, relentlessly, persistently, with the inexhaustible energy of a baby who knows exactly what he wants, was the boxes.

"Grandfather, I want to see the boxes."

"No, grandchild. You must not touch them."

"Grandfather, please. Just one box. Just to hold."

"No, grandchild."

The child cried. He cried all night, his wail rising through the cedar walls of the house, shaking the roof beams. He cried all day, his tears running down his face in rivers, his fists clenched, his voice hoarse but unrelenting. The chief could not sleep. The household could not function. The daughter begged her father to give the child what he wanted.

At last, worn down by the crying, the chief relented. He brought out the first box — the largest — and opened it.

The stars burst free. They flew from the box like sparks from a fire, swirling upward, embedding themselves in the dark sky. The world flickered with faint light — the first light it had known.

But the child wanted more. He cried for the second box, and the chief opened it, and the moon rose out of it like a silver fish jumping from the water, climbing the sky, casting its pale glow over the world.

The child wanted the third box. The chief opened it, and the northern lights — the aurora — spilled out, painting the sky with curtains of green and violet and white, rippling like fabric in a wind that blew from the edge of the world.

Now the child stopped crying. He held the remaining two boxes — the smallest, the most tightly sealed — and the chief watched with growing unease, for he knew that the last box held the greatest treasure.

The child fumbled with the seals. The chief tried to stop him, but it was too late. The child tore open the final box, and the sun — the blazing, golden, world-illuminating sun — erupted from his hands. In the same instant, the child transformed. His body stretched and darkened, his arms became wings, his beak lengthened, and he was Raven again — not a baby, not a trickster in disguise, but Raven in his true form, black as the night he was about to destroy.

Raven seized the sun in his beak and flew. He flew up, up, past the smoke hole of the chief's house, past the clouds, past the stars he had released, into the sky itself. And there he released the sun, placing it in the highest reaches of the heavens, where it blazed forth and flooded the world with daylight.

The darkness was over. The world could see.

This myth — told by the Nuu-chah-nulth and by peoples across the Pacific Northwest in variations that differ in detail but agree in essence — establishes Raven as the primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night. Light, in the Nuu-chah-nulth understanding, was not given freely by the gods. It was stolen, tricked, wrested from the clutches of those who would hoard it. And it was Raven — selfish, clever, insatiable Raven — who brought it to the people, not because he loved them, but because he wanted to see where he was going.

title: Raven Annoys Octopus (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit and watch the ocean. They saw a woman walking along the beach with her hair long and strung into eight braids — she was Octopus, carrying a digging stick to look for clams. She sat down on a rock and began to dig. Soon another person came along the beach, tall with glossy black hair — it was Raven. The old people predicted he would bother Octopus, and they knew it was not a good idea. Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat and began bothering her. He teased and pestered her while she tried to dig for clams. The story serves as a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, teaching him (and the listener) that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; native-languages.org
full_text:
One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit on the warm rocks and watch the ocean. This was what old people did in the villages along the coast — they watched the water, they talked about the weather, they remembered things that had happened when the world was younger. The tide was low, and the rocks were dry, and the morning sun was warm on their faces.

They saw a woman walking along the beach. She was alone, and she moved with a steady, purposeful stride. Her hair was long — very long — strung into eight braids that hung down her back like dark ropes. She carried a digging stick in one hand, and she was looking for clams.

The old people recognized her. She was Octopus — not a human woman but a spirit-being who took human form when she came to the shore to dig for clams. Her eight braids were the eight arms she would reveal if she chose to, and her digging stick was the tool she used to pry clams from the sand.

Octopus sat down on a flat rock near the water's edge and began to dig. She worked slowly, methodically, pushing the stick into the wet sand, prying up the surface, finding the clams beneath. She was absorbed in her work, and she did not notice the figure approaching along the beach.

He was tall, with glossy black hair that caught the light like oil on water. His step was light, almost dancing, and there was a smirk on his face that the old people recognized immediately.

"That's Raven," one of them muttered. "And he's going to bother her."

The others nodded. They had seen this before. Raven could not leave anyone in peace. If someone was working, Raven wanted to interfere. If someone was happy, Raven wanted to make them unhappy. If someone was sitting quietly on a rock digging for clams, Raven wanted to make their life miserable.

Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat. He did not announce himself. He did not greet her with the proper words. He simply walked up and began talking — nonsense, mostly, the kind of restless, probing chatter that Raven used when he was bored and looking for amusement.

"What are you doing?" he asked, though it was obvious.

"Digging clams," Octopus said, not looking up.

"Why?"

"To eat."

"What kind of clams?"

"The kind that live in the sand."

"I know that. But what kind?"

Octopus ignored him. She dug another clam from the sand and placed it in her basket.

Raven leaned closer. He peered into the hole she had dug. He nudged her arm with his elbow. He picked up a handful of sand and let it trickle through his fingers. He made comments about her technique, her braids, her stick, the quality of the clams, the state of the tide.

The old people on the rocks shook their heads. They knew how this would end. Raven never learned. He never understood that bothering people was wrong, or that persistence in irritation was not the same as charm. He would keep pestering Octopus until she had enough, and then there would be consequences.

The story — told along the coast from village to village, generation to generation — is a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, as it always does, teaching him and the listener that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs, even when those affairs are none of his business.

title: Kwatyat and Tihtipihin Rescue Their Mother (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Two Nuu-chah-nulth brothers, Tihtipihin and Kwatyat, witnessed a great monster swallow their mother whole. Without hesitation, they willingly allowed themselves to be swallowed by the same monster so they could rescue her. Inside the monster's stomach, they found their mother alive along with other swallowed victims. Using their wits and supernatural strength, the brothers cut through the monster's stomach from the inside, freeing themselves, their mother, and all the other captives. They escaped safely as the monster perished. This story of filial devotion and brotherly courage is one of the most important Nuu-chah-nulth hero tales. Kwatyat, the younger brother, is particularly significant as he is recognized as a transformer figure in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology who later helped shape the world. The story emphasizes family loyalty, bravery in the face of overwhelming danger, and the power of cooperation between siblings.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; Wikipedia
full_text:
Two brothers — Tihtipihin, the elder, and Kwatyat, the younger — were walking through the forest when they saw something that stopped them cold. A great monster, vast and terrible, with a mouth that could swallow a whale and teeth like canoe paddles, opened its throat and swallowed their mother whole.

She was gone in an instant. One moment she was walking between them, her hand on Kwatyat's shoulder, her voice telling a story about the old days. The next moment the monster's jaws had closed around her, and she was inside its belly, and the brothers were standing alone on the forest trail.

There was no time for grief. No time for planning. Tihtipihin looked at Kwatyat, and Kwatyat looked at Tihtipihin, and without a word they made the decision that defined them as heroes.

They walked into the monster's mouth.

The darkness inside was absolute. The walls of the creature's throat were slick and warm, and the air smelled of rot and stomach acid. They slid downward, tumbling through the dark, until they landed on something soft — the floor of the monster's stomach, where the remains of previous meals lay in various stages of digestion.

And there, in the dim, wet darkness, they found their mother. She was alive — barely — but alive. And with her were other swallowed victims: a fisherman, a hunter, an old woman, a child. All of them had been eaten by the monster. All of them had given up hope of escape.

But the brothers had not given up. Kwatyat, the younger, was the clever one. He carried a knife — a blade of sharpened bone that he kept in his belt for cutting rope and preparing food. He drew the knife and began to cut.

The monster's stomach wall was thick and tough, like the hide of a whale, but the knife was sharp and Kwatyat's arm was strong. He cut and cut, and Tihtipihin held the flesh steady, and slowly, agonizingly, they carved an opening large enough for a person to crawl through.

One by one, they helped the swallowed victims out through the hole in the monster's side. The fisherman first, then the hunter, then the old woman, then the child. Their mother came last, supported by Tihtipihin's arm, her face pale but her eyes fierce with the determination of a woman who had been swallowed by a monster and was not pleased about it.

They all escaped into the daylight, and the monster, its belly torn open, perished where it lay.

The story of the two brothers who rescued their mother from the monster is one of the most important Nuu-chah-nulth hero tales. It is a story of filial devotion — of sons who loved their mother so deeply that they were willing to be swallowed by a monster to save her. It is a story of brotherly courage — of two young men who did not hesitate, who did not argue, who did not weigh the risks, but acted immediately and decisively.

Kwatyat, the younger brother, is particularly significant in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. After the rescue of his mother, he went on to become one of the great transformer figures — beings who traveled the land, correcting what was wrong, shaping the world for the people who would come after. His first act of transformation was the most important: he transformed the dead monster into a landmark — a distinctive rock formation that still stands on the coast, a reminder that even the most terrible monsters can be defeated by courage and cooperation between siblings.

title: Andaokut Rescues the Children (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: A woman whose children had been stolen by Malahas, a malicious forest goddess, wept uncontrollably. From her mucus or tears, a child was born — Andaokut. This miraculous birth child grew with extraordinary speed and possessed supernatural abilities. Andaokut set out to rescue the stolen children, tracking Malahas to her remote forest lair. Using courage and cleverness, he confronted Malahas and defeated her, freeing all the children she had captured. He killed Malahas and returned the children safely to their families. This story from Nuu-chah-nulth tradition exemplifies the theme of miraculous birth and the triumph of good over evil. Andaokut represents hope born from despair, showing that even from a mother's tears, salvation can emerge. The defeat of Malahas demonstrates that even the most powerful evil beings can be overcome by determination and courage.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; Wikipedia
full_text:
Malahas was a goddess of the forest, but not the kind of goddess that brought comfort or blessing. She was malicious, cunning, and hungry — a being who stole children from their homes and carried them to her remote forest lair, where she kept them in cages of woven branch and fed them on berries that tasted sweet but left them drowsy and confused.

The mothers of the village wept. Their children were gone — taken in the night, vanished without a trace, leaving only a trail of small footprints that led into the deep woods and then disappeared. The hunters searched. The shamans called on the spirits. But Malahas was clever, and her forest was vast, and the children were nowhere to be found.

One woman wept more than the others. Her children — two of them, a boy and a girl — had been taken on the same night, and her grief was so deep that it consumed her entirely. She could not eat. She could not sleep. She sat by the door of her house and wept, her tears falling like rain, her mucus dripping from her nose in long, glistening threads.

And from those tears — from the mucus and the grief — something miraculous happened. A child was born.

He was small at first, barely the size of a newborn, but he grew with extraordinary speed. In a single day he went from infant to toddler, from toddler to child, from child to young man. And as he grew, he acquired abilities that no ordinary human possessed: strength beyond measure, speed beyond catching, and a knowledge of the forest that surpassed even Malahas's own.

The woman named him Andaokut. And Andaokut told her, on the day he reached his full height: "I will bring your children back."

He walked into the forest. He did not need to track Malahas — he could feel her presence like a heat on the wind, like a sourness in the air. He followed the feeling through the dense woods, past trees so thick that their trunks blocked out the sky, past rivers that ran black with tannin, past clearings where the silence was so complete that the sound of his own breathing was deafening.

He found Malahas's lair at the center of the forest — a place of twisted trees and dim light, where the cages of woven branches held not only the children of his mother's village but children from a dozen other villages, all of them drowsy, all of them confused, all of them waiting for rescue.

Malahas was there. She was enormous — taller than the trees, with skin like bark and eyes like knots in wood. When she saw Andaokut, she laughed. "Another child," she said. "Come to be caged."

But Andaokut was no child. He confronted Malahas with the full force of his supernatural power, and the battle that followed shook the forest to its roots. Trees fell. The ground cracked. The sky darkened with the force of their struggle.

In the end, Andaokut prevailed. He killed Malahas and broke open every cage in the lair, freeing all the stolen children. He led them out of the forest — a long procession of thin, dazed boys and girls, blinking in the sunlight — and returned them to their families.

The story from Nuu-chah-nulth tradition exemplifies the theme of miraculous birth and the triumph of good over evil. Andaokut represents hope born from despair, showing that even from a mother's tears, salvation can emerge. The defeat of Malahas demonstrates that even the most powerful evil beings can be overcome by determination, courage, and the supernatural gifts that come from a love deep enough to create life from grief.

title: Matlose the Hobgoblin (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Matlose is the most feared hobgoblin spirit of the Nuu-chah-nulth people, described as a monstrous Caliban-like creature. His head resembles something that might have been human but is not, and his uncouth bulk is horrid with black bristles. His monstrous teeth and curved claws are like those of a bear, capable of rending prey into morsels with a single stroke. Most terrifying of all is his voice — whoever hears Matlose's terrible voice falls as if smitten, paralyzed by fear. He lurks in the deep forests and remote mountains of Vancouver Island, preying on anyone who ventures too far from the safety of the village. Shamans and warriors who successfully confront Matlose gain immense supernatural power. The Matlose legend serves as both a cautionary tale about the dangers of the wilderness and a testament to the power of the spirit world that surrounds the Nuu-chah-nulth people.
source: Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition; native-languages.org
full_text:
Of all the spirits that haunt the forests and mountains of Vancouver Island, none is more feared than Matlose. The Nuu-chah-nulth people speak his name reluctantly, if they speak it at all, for Matlose is the most terrible hobgoblin in their tradition — a creature so hideous, so powerful, so utterly without mercy that even the bravest warriors prefer to avoid the places where he dwells.

Matlose is a monstrous being — Caliban-like in his deformity, a thing of nightmare given flesh and hunger. His head resembles something that might once have been human, in the way that a stone might once have been a river — you can see the memory of its origin, but the transformation has been so complete that the original is barely recognizable. His face is a ruin of features: a flat nose, deep-set eyes that glow like embers, a mouth that stretches too wide and is filled with teeth like broken obsidian.

His body is horrid with black bristles — thick, coarse hairs that grow from every inch of his skin, so that he appears to be wearing a coat of dark fur. His uncouth bulk moves through the forest with a terrible, lurching gait, his massive shoulders brushing aside trees as if they were reeds. His hands are enormous, and his curved claws — like those of a bear, but longer, sharper, and black as pitch — are capable of rending prey into morsels with a single stroke.

But the worst thing about Matlose is his voice.

Whoever hears Matlose's terrible voice falls as if smitten. The sound is not a roar or a scream but something else — a vibration that enters the body through the bones, through the blood, through the marrow itself, paralyzing every muscle, freezing every thought. The victim stands rooted to the spot, unable to flee, unable to fight, unable even to close their eyes as Matlose approaches with his great clawed hands reaching.

Matlose lurks in the deep forests and remote mountains of Vancouver Island, in places where the trees grow so thick that even in summer the ground is dark, where the moss hangs in curtains from the branches, where the silence is broken only by the sound of dripping water and the occasional crack of a falling limb. He preys on anyone who ventures too far from the safety of the village — hunters who stray from the trail, children who wander into the woods, travelers who camp in the wrong place.

Shamans and warriors who successfully confront Matlose gain immense supernatural power. The encounter is a test — the ultimate test — of a person's spiritual strength. Those who face Matlose and survive carry the mark of their victory for the rest of their lives: a strength in their voice, a power in their hands, a certainty in their spirit that comes from having looked into the face of the most terrible being in the Nuu-chah-nulth world and not flinching.

The Matlose legend serves as both a cautionary tale about the dangers of the wilderness and a testament to the power of the spirit world that surrounds the Nuu-chah-nulth people. The forest is not empty. The mountains are not safe. And there are beings in the world whose very voice can destroy you.

title: The Theft of Light (Tsimshian - Weeget)
summary: On Raven's first journey, Weeget (Giant/Raven) flew inland toward the east carrying a stone his father the chief had given him. When exhausted, he dropped the stone on the sea, where it became a large rock. At that time there was always darkness — no daylight existed. Weeget put on his raven skin and scattered salmon and trout roe into every river and creek, declaring that all waters should have fish. He then flew up through a hole in the sky to reach heaven. Near the chief of heaven's house, he found a spring where the chief's daughter drank. He turned into a floating object, was swallowed, and was born as a human child. He stole the light (called maa) and escaped back to earth. When the Frog people at the Nass River mocked him while fishing for olachen and refused his requests, Weeget broke the maa, releasing daylight. The north wind drove the Frogs away, and they froze onto a rock where they remain as stone to this day. Thus the Tsimshian explain the origin of daylight.
source: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; Tsimshian oral tradition
full_text:
On Raven's first journey, Weeget — Giant/Raven — flew inland toward the east carrying a stone his father the chief had given him. The stone was smooth and heavy, and it was meant to mark the place where Weeget would return. When exhausted, he dropped the stone on the sea, where it became a large rock — a landmark that could be seen from both land and water, a reminder of the giant's journey.

At that time there was always darkness — no daylight existed. The world was lit only by the firelight of the longhouses and the faint glow of the stars, which were small and dim. Weeget put on his raven skin and scattered salmon and trout roe into every river and creek, declaring that all waters should have fish. This was his first gift to the world — the abundance of the sea, brought to the rivers.

He then flew up through a hole in the sky to reach heaven. The hole was small, and Weeget was large, and he had to squeeze through it, his wings scraping the edges, his feathers ruffling in the thin air. On the other side was the house of the chief of heaven — a great longhouse, its posts carved with the images of celestial beings, its roof open to the stars.

Near the chief's house, he found a spring where the chief's daughter drank. He turned into a floating object — something that bobbed on the surface of the water, unremarkable, ordinary. She drank, and she swallowed him, and she became pregnant.

She gave birth to Weeget as a human child. He stole the light — called maa — and escaped back to earth. The maa was a small, bright object, no larger than a man's fist, but it burned with a light that was warmer and brighter than any fire.

When the Frog people at the Nass River mocked him while fishing for olachen and refused his requests, Weeget broke the maa, releasing daylight. The north wind drove the Frogs away, and they froze onto a rock where they remain as stone to this day. The light spread across the world, turning night into day, and the people looked up and saw, for the first time, the green of the trees, the blue of the water, the brown of the earth.

title: The Story of Asdiwal (Tsimshian)
summary: Asdiwal is one of the most important Tsimshian hero narratives, recorded in multiple versions by Franz Boas. The story begins with a mother and daughter dying of starvation during a winter famine in the Skeena River region. A supernatural being named Hatsenas (a bird of good omen) appears, provides food, and fathers Asdiwal with the younger woman. Hatsenas gives his son magical objects including a never-missing bow, invisible-making hat, and inexhaustible food basket. Asdiwal's adventures include hunting a magical bear up to the sky, where the bear transforms into Evening-Star, daughter of the Sun. He marries her after passing deadly trials set by the Sun. Returning to earth, Asdiwal marries a Tsimshian chief's daughter and becomes wealthy through potlatches. He competes with his brothers-in-law in sea-lion hunting but is abandoned on a reef during a storm. His father saves him. Eventually Asdiwal goes mountain hunting without his snowshoes, gets lost, and is turned to stone with his dog and lance — a transformation that can still be seen on a mountain at Ginadâos Lake.
source: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Texts (1895, 1902, 1912); Tsimshian oral tradition recorded by Henry Tate
full_text:
Asdiwal is one of the most important Tsimshian hero narratives, recorded in multiple versions by Franz Boas. The story begins with a mother and daughter dying of starvation during a winter famine in the Skeena River region. The village was empty, the food stores depleted, and the people had nothing left but memories of better times.

A supernatural being named Hatsenas — a bird of good omen, with feathers that shimmered like copper — appeared, provided food, and fathered Asdiwal with the younger woman. Hatsenas gave his son magical objects including a never-missing bow, an invisible-making hat, and an inexhaustible food basket.

Asdiwal's adventures included hunting a magical bear up to the sky, where the bear transformed into Evening-Star, daughter of the Sun. He married her after passing deadly trials set by the Sun — trials of strength, courage, and wisdom. Returning to earth, Asdiwal married a Tsimshian chief's daughter and became wealthy through potlatches.

He competed with his brothers-in-law in sea-lion hunting but was abandoned on a reef during a storm. His father saved him. Eventually Asdiwal went mountain hunting without his snowshoes, got lost, and is turned to stone with his dog and lance — a transformation that can still be seen on a mountain at Ginados Lake.

The stone figures are visible from a distance: a man standing upright, a dog at his side, a lance in his hand. They are gray and weathered, shaped by centuries of rain and wind, but they are unmistakably human. The Tsimshian point to them and tell the story of Asdiwal — the hero who reached the sky, who married the daughter of the Sun, who lost everything and gained everything, and who was turned to stone for his hubris.

title: Raven Becomes Voracious (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from salmon to berries, from seal meat to olachen grease. His hunger became so legendary that it defined his character. The story serves as an etiological myth explaining why ravens and crows are scavengers who eat constantly and are always hungry. It also carries a moral lesson about the dangers of greed and insatiable desire. Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled. The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure.
source: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; Tsimshian oral tradition
full_text:
This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. He was clever, yes, and mischievous, but he was not the creature of endless appetite that he would become.

Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from salmon to berries, from seal meat to olachen grease. His hunger became so legendary that it defined his character — he was no longer simply Raven the trickster; he was Raven the hungry, Raven the devourer, Raven who could never be satisfied.

The story serves as an etiological myth explaining why ravens and crows are scavengers who eat constantly and are always hungry. The birds peck at garbage, at carcasses, at anything that might contain a morsel of food, because Raven's hunger lives in them — an eternal, unsatisfiable need that drives them to eat and eat and eat.

It also carries a moral lesson about the dangers of greed and insatiable desire. Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food, his plans becoming more elaborate and more ridiculous with each attempt — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled.

The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure. Raven brings gifts to the people — light, fish, fire — but he also brings trouble, and his hunger is the source of both his generosity and his destruction.

title: Wolf Clan and the Salmon (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals — he did not welcome the salmon chief properly, did not prepare the first salmon with the required ceremony, and showed disrespect to the salmon people. In response, the supernatural forces beneath the mountains grew angry. A great volcanic eruption occurred, devastating the land and reminding all Tsimshian people of the sacred obligation to honor the salmon. The story reinforces the fundamental Northwest Coast principle that humans and salmon are in a reciprocal relationship: humans must treat salmon with respect or face catastrophic consequences. It also explains volcanic activity in the Nass and Skeena River regions through the lens of spiritual cause and effect.
source: Tsimshian oral tradition; native-languages.org
full_text:
This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. The first salmon was a gift from the salmon people, and it demanded proper treatment — a welcome ceremony, a respectful preparation, a careful distribution of the flesh.

One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals. He did not welcome the salmon chief properly, did not prepare the first salmon with the required ceremony, and showed disrespect to the salmon people. He cut the fish carelessly, discarded the head and bones, and cooked it without the proper prayers.

In response, the supernatural forces beneath the mountains grew angry. The earth trembled. Smoke rose from the peaks. A great volcanic eruption occurred, devastating the land — the lava flow destroyed the village, the ash cloud darkened the sky, and the rivers ran hot with melted rock.

The eruption reminded all Tsimshian people of the sacred obligation to honor the salmon. The story reinforces the fundamental Northwest Coast principle that humans and salmon are in a reciprocal relationship: humans must treat salmon with respect or face catastrophic consequences.

The salmon are not simply food; they are people — the salmon people, who return to the rivers each year to give themselves to the humans. To disrespect the salmon is to disrespect the gift, and to disrespect the gift is to invite the wrath of the spirits who control the natural world.

It also explains volcanic activity in the Nass and Skeena River regions through the lens of spiritual cause and effect. The volcanoes are not simply geological features; they are the anger of the salmon people, expressed through the fire and stone of the earth.

title: The Porcupine and the Beaver (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth from the William Beynon collection tells of a time when animals spoke like human beings and possessed great powers to change the weather. Porcupine and Beaver, two animal-people, had a contest of abilities that determined their roles in the world. Porcupine demonstrated his cleverness and defensive capabilities, while Beaver showed his industrious nature and engineering skills. The story carries important teachings about using one's natural gifts wisely and respecting the different abilities of others. It is also an etiological tale explaining the physical characteristics and behaviors of both porcupines and beavers. Porcupine's quills and Beaver's tail receive supernatural explanations in the narrative. Recorded by William Beynon, a Tsimshian ethnographer who worked with Franz Boas, this story represents one of the many animal-person tales that convey moral teachings while explaining the natural world.
source: William Beynon, Tsimshian Stories; Columbia University Library
full_text:
This Tsimshian myth from the William Beynon collection tells of a time when animals spoke like human beings and possessed great powers to change the weather. Porcupine and Beaver, two animal-people, had a contest of abilities that determined their roles in the world.

Porcupine demonstrated his cleverness and defensive capabilities. He showed how his quills could be used as weapons — sharp, barbed, painful — and how they could be used as tools — needles, pins, fishhooks. He showed how his ability to curl into a ball protected him from predators, how his quiet movement through the forest allowed him to observe without being observed.

Beaver showed his industrious nature and engineering skills. He demonstrated how he could fell a tree with his teeth, how he could build a dam that held back a river, how he could create a pond that provided food and shelter for many animals. He showed how his flat tail could be used as a tool — a hammer for pounding stakes, a rudder for swimming, a signal for warning others of danger.

The story carries important teachings about using one's natural gifts wisely and respecting the different abilities of others. Neither Porcupine nor Beaver is superior; each has a unique set of skills, and each contributes to the world in a way that the other cannot.

It is also an etiological tale explaining the physical characteristics and behaviors of both porcupines and beavers. Porcupine's quills and Beaver's tail receive supernatural explanations in the narrative — gifts from the Creator, earned through the contest of abilities.

Recorded by William Beynon, a Tsimshian ethnographer who worked with Franz Boas, this story represents one of the many animal-person tales that convey moral teachings while explaining the natural world.

title: The Four Carpenters and the Creation of the World (Nuxalk)
summary: When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels. They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq (the Milky Way). There were 45 original families, each with their own room in the House of Smayusta (the Creator's house in the upper world). The ancestors were given cwmnwas (spirit) placed in the bone of the back of their neck, and slhup'tsta (breath). They were given names, food, tools, a code of ethics, and protocols, all placed within a nuslhiixwta (treasure box). Hanging on the walls were animal, bird, and sea creature cloaks. Each ancestor chose a cloak — grizzly bear, raven, eagle, killer whale, wolf, mountain goat, heron — and danced with it. The Creator threw his sun blanket over himself and transformed into the sun. The ancestors did the same, transforming into their chosen animals. Guided by the eyelashes of the sun, they floated down to earth and removed their cloaks, which returned to heaven. This is the Nuxalk creation story, explaining the origin of all Nuxalk clans and their crests.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation official website
full_text:
When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels, beings of light and purpose who moved through the air with the ease of birds.

They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq — the Milky Way, the great spiral of stars that stretches across the sky. The tree was vast beyond imagining, its branches reaching from one end of the sky to the other, its roots plunging into the depths of the ocean. From its wood, the Four Carpenters carved the first humans — forty-five original families, each with their own room in the House of Smayusta, the Creator's house in the upper world.

The ancestors were given cwmnwas — spirit — placed in the bone of the back of their neck, and slhup'tsta — breath. They were given names, food, tools, a code of ethics, and protocols, all placed within a nuslhiixwta — a treasure box, a container of cultural knowledge that each family carried with them.

Hanging on the walls of the House of Smayusta were animal, bird, and sea creature cloaks — garments of power, each one representing a different aspect of the natural world. Each ancestor chose a cloak — grizzly bear, raven, eagle, killer whale, wolf, mountain goat, heron — and danced with it, absorbing its power, learning its ways.

The Creator threw his sun blanket over himself and transformed into the sun. The ancestors did the same, transforming into their chosen animals. Guided by the eyelashes of the sun, they floated down to earth and removed their cloaks, which returned to heaven. The ancestors remained in their animal forms, and from them came the clans of the Nuxalk — each clan bearing the name and the crest of the animal it had chosen.

This is the Nuxalk creation story, explaining the origin of all Nuxalk clans and their crests.

title: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)
summary: In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata (the land above) and let no one see it. The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life. They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven. The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down, then a hemlock needle, but she blew him away. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in. She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. Raven cried for the box holding the light until Alhkw'ntam gave in. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon. The people were no longer sad.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation official website; Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians
full_text:
In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata, the land above, and let no one see it. The box was locked, and the key was hidden, and the people's prayers went unanswered.

The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird — small, black, and ordinary. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life.

They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven.

The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down — soft, white, drifting — but she blew him away. Then he transformed into a hemlock needle — small, sharp, ordinary — but she blew him away again. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in.

She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. The child cried incessantly, his voice high and piercing, until Alhkw'ntam gave in and offered him the box holding the light. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon.

The people were no longer sad. They looked up and saw the light — warm, bright, beautiful — and they celebrated the gift that Raven had brought them.

This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.

title: The Story of Ista (Nuxalk)
summary: Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus (King Island) in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast. Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her story is part of the Nuxalk understanding of how the first ancestors established territories and rights to the land. Traditional family names are handed down and validated at potlatches. The Ista story also includes the tale of Patsallht (First Born), who thought he was the only one on earth. He was given a medicine box containing a 'mukw' of shame, stubbornness, and jealousy. He met the Sisawk people (Society of Chiefs) but was ashamed he was not a member. Later, he met a beautiful woman wearing a red blanket who proposed marriage. She was a grizzly bear woman who built him a home from hemlock. When she left him, First Born refused to leave the house. People followed his puppy to find him and convinced him to feast with them by offering to paint their faces black. The Ista people were ultimately wiped out by a cannibal raiding party from far away.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Skwucwlikwana (Lucy Mack); Nuxalk Nation
full_text:
Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus — King Island — in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast, her movements graceful and purposeful, her blanket shimmering with the iridescent light of the shell.

Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her dance was not entertainment; it was a declaration, a statement of identity, a way of marking the land with her presence. Everywhere she danced, she left behind a trace of her spirit — in the rocks, in the trees, in the water itself.

Her story is part of the Nuxalk understanding of how the first ancestors established territories and rights to the land. Traditional family names are handed down and validated at potlatches — the great ceremonies where wealth is distributed, histories are recited, and rights are affirmed. To hold a name is to hold a connection to the land, and to validate that name at a potlatch is to renew the connection.

The Ista story also includes the tale of Patsallht — First Born — who thought he was the only one on earth. He was given a medicine box containing a 'mukw' of shame, stubbornness, and jealousy — three human failings that would shape his character and his interactions with others.

He met the Sisawk people — the Society of Chiefs — but was ashamed he was not a member. Later, he met a beautiful woman wearing a red blanket who proposed marriage. She was a grizzly bear woman who built him a home from hemlock, her paws shaping the wood with a precision that rivaled any human carpenter.

When she left him, First Born refused to leave the house. People followed his puppy to find him and convinced him to feast with them by offering to paint their faces black — a gesture of mourning that was also a gesture of welcome.

The Ista people were ultimately wiped out by a cannibal raiding party from far away. Their story is a reminder that even the most powerful lineages can be destroyed, and that the land remembers those who once walked upon it.

title: The Sun Tests His Son-in-Law (Nuxalk)
summary: In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice and subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests. The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one. Salmon Boy succeeded with the help of his wife. Next, the Sun required him to draw water from a spring whose walls closed in on anyone who approached. Again his wife helped him. The Sun tried to bake him in a supernaturally hot sweat lodge, burn him on hot stones, and crush him with a falling tree. Each time Salmon Boy survived through his wife's guidance and his own growing supernatural power. Finally recognizing his son-in-law's worth, the Sun accepted him and bestowed upon him the gift of bringing salmon to the people. Salmon Boy returned to earth as a powerful being who taught the Nuxalk people how to properly catch, prepare, and honor the salmon, establishing the sacred relationship between the people and the salmon runs.
source: Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians; Nuxalk oral tradition
full_text:
In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice — Salmon Boy was mortal, poor, and unremarkable — and he subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests.

The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one. The mountain was so steep that the goats climbed on their hind legs, their hooves finding purchase in cracks no wider than a finger. Salmon Boy succeeded with the help of his wife, who told him where to stand and when to throw.

Next, the Sun required him to draw water from a spring whose walls closed in on anyone who approached. The walls were made of stone, and they moved — slowly, inexorably — like the jaws of a great beast. Again his wife helped him, telling him when to reach in and when to pull back.

The Sun tried to bake him in a supernaturally hot sweat lodge, burn him on hot stones, and crush him with a falling tree. Each time Salmon Boy survived through his wife's guidance and his own growing supernatural power. He was learning, with each trial, to harness the forces that the Sun controlled.

Finally recognizing his son-in-law's worth, the Sun accepted him and bestowed upon him the gift of bringing salmon to the people. Salmon Boy returned to earth as a powerful being who taught the Nuxalk people how to properly catch, prepare, and honor the salmon, establishing the sacred relationship between the people and the salmon runs.

The tests of the Sun are not simply trials of strength; they are initiations. Each test stripped away a layer of Salmon Boy's humanity and replaced it with something greater — knowledge, power, connection to the natural world.
